Step 1Core Python · Getting started

1.1

What a program is and your first Python program

Open chapter

Programs, compiler and interpreter, CPython, REPL and scripts, print() with sep and end, keywords, indentation, error kinds, PEP 8.

Key ideas

  • Program and language A program is a list of exact instructions. Lexis is the vocabulary, syntax the grammar, semantics the meaning.
  • How CPython runs a file Source is checked and compiled to bytecode, then the virtual machine runs it top to bottom. A SyntaxError anywhere stops everything.
  • print() print(*values, sep=" ", end="\n"). str() on each value, sep between, end after. N = L + (n − 1)s + e.
  • Keywords and blocks 35 keywords in 3.14, soft keywords match, case, type, _. # starts a comment. Indent blocks with 4 spaces.
  • Three errors Syntax error before running, runtime error at the bad line, logic error never reported.

Formulas

The full form of print()Exam favourite
print(*values, sep=" ", end="\n", file=sys.stdout, flush=False)
values: any number of values. sep: text between them. end: text after the last one. file: where to write. flush: write at once.
Lesson: print(): showing results on the screen
Characters written by one print()Exam favourite
N = ∑ len(str(vi)) + (n − 1) · len(sep) + len(end)
n values v1 to vn. There are n − 1 gaps between n values.
Lesson: print(): showing results on the screen
Characters from one print()Exam favourite
N = L + (n − 1) · s + e
L = total length of all values as text, n = number of values, s = len(sep), e = len(end).
Lesson: The maths: counting what print() writes
Bytes in a plain English text file
bytes = characters
Each English letter, digit, space and new line is 1 byte in UTF-8. Letters from other scripts can take 2 to 4 bytes (Core 3.1).
Lesson: The maths: counting what print() writes

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Python is often called an interpreted language, but CPython does compile your code to bytecode first. Both words are partly true. The Advanced Python step 7 chapter "How Python runs" opens every one of these stages with an animation.Lesson: Compiler, interpreter and how Python runs your file
  • Common mistake
    In the REPL, typing 2 + 3 shows 5 without print(). In a .py file, nothing appears unless you call print(). Beginners often expect the REPL behaviour inside a file.Lesson: Install Python and run your first program
  • In the exam
    sep and end must be given by name (keyword arguments). print("A", "B", "-") prints A B - with the dash as a third value, it does not change sep.Lesson: print(): showing results on the screen
  • Common mistake
    Python uses indentation where many languages use curly brackets. Mixing tabs and spaces, or using 3 spaces on one line and 4 on the next, gives IndentationError. PEP 8 says: always 4 spaces.Lesson: Keywords, statements, comments and indentation
  • In the exam
    PCEP asks which names follow PEP 8 conventions. snake_case for variables and functions, CapWords for classes, UPPER_CASE for constants.Lesson: Writing code other people can read: PEP 8 and PEP 20
1.2

Variables, values, types and numeral systems

Open chapter

Names and objects, the basic types and literals, numeral systems, type conversion, naming rules, multiple assignment.

Key ideas

  • Names and objects name = value binds a name to an object. b = a gives a second name to the same object. Objects have id, type, value.
  • Basic types int (unlimited), float (about 15 to 17 digits), complex, bool (subclass of int), str, None. All immutable.
  • Bases 0b, 0o, 0x literals. bin(), oct(), hex() to text. int(text, base) back. N = sum of di bi.
  • Conversions int() cuts towards zero, int("3.5") is ValueError, round() ties to even, bool("0") is True.
  • Naming Letters, digits, _ , no leading digit, no keyword, case sensitive, snake_case, do not shadow built ins.

Formulas

Scientific notationExam favourite
a e b = a × 10b
1.5e3 = 1.5 × 103 = 1500.0. The result is always a float.
Lesson: The basic data types and their literals
Underscores in numbers
1_000_000 == 1000000
Since Python 3.6 (PEP 515) underscores can group digits. Python ignores them.
Lesson: The basic data types and their literals
Value of a number written in base bExam favourite
value = dkbk + ... + d1b1 + d0b0
Each digit is multiplied by the base to the power of its position, counting from 0 on the right.
Lesson: Numeral systems: binary, octal and hexadecimal
Digits needed in base 2
bits(n) = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1
For n > 0. Python gives it as n.bit_length(). 156 needs 8 bits.
Lesson: Numeral systems: binary, octal and hexadecimal
Base b to decimalExam favourite
N = ∑i=0k di · bi
di is the digit at position i from the right.
Lesson: The maths: place value and conversions
Decimal to base bExam favourite
d0 = N mod b, N ← N // b, repeat
The remainders in reverse order are the digits.
Lesson: The maths: place value and conversions
Largest number in k bits
2k − 1
8 bits hold 0 to 255. 16 bits hold 0 to 65,535.
Lesson: The maths: place value and conversions
One hex digit
= 4 bits, one octal digit = 3 bits
So 0xFF is 1111 1111 and 0o7 is 111.
Lesson: The maths: place value and conversions

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    In Python a variable has no type of its own. The object has the type. The same name can point to an int now and to a str later. This is called dynamic typing.Lesson: What a variable really is
  • In the exam
    bool is a kind of int: True == 1 and False == 0, so True + True is 2. This surprises many people in exams.Lesson: The basic data types and their literals
  • Common mistake
    A leading zero is not allowed on a decimal literal in Python 3: 017 is a SyntaxError. Write 0o17 for octal.Lesson: Numeral systems: binary, octal and hexadecimal
  • In the exam
    int(-3.99) is -3, not -4. int() cuts towards zero. math.floor(-3.99) is -4 because floor goes down.Lesson: Changing one type into another
  • Common mistake
    Naming a variable list or str hides the built in. After list = [1, 2], calling list("abc") fails with TypeError: 'list' object is not callable.Lesson: Naming rules and good names
1.3

Operators, expressions and the order Python works them out

Open chapter

Arithmetic, // and %, precedence, comparisons, float precision, logic and short circuit, bitwise operators.

Key ideas

  • Division / gives float. // floors (towards minus infinity). % has the sign of the divisor. a == (a // b) * b + a % b.
  • Priority brackets, **, unary, * / // %, + -, shifts, & ^ |, comparisons, not, and, or. ** right to left. -2 ** 2 = -4.
  • Comparisons Chained 1 < x < 10. Floats: use math.isclose(). 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False.
  • Logic and, or short circuit and return an operand. not > and > or.
  • Bits ~x = -x - 1. x << k = x * 2**k. x & 1 tests odd. x & (x - 1) == 0 tests power of 2.

Formulas

True division
a / b
Always gives a float: 6 / 3 = 2.0.
Lesson: Arithmetic: the seven number operators
Floor divisionExam favourite
a // b = ⌊a ÷ b⌋
Divide, then round down towards minus infinity. 7 // 2 = 3, -7 // 2 = -4.
Lesson: Arithmetic: the seven number operators
Remainder (modulo)Exam favourite
a % b = a − b · (a // b)
Has the same sign as b. -7 % 2 = 1.
Lesson: Arithmetic: the seven number operators
The division identityExam favourite
a == (a // b) * b + a % b
Always true in Python for b ≠ 0. Use it to check your answers.
Lesson: Arithmetic: the seven number operators
Safe float comparisonExam favourite
|a − b| ≤ max(rel · max(|a|, |b|), abs_tol)
This is math.isclose(a, b). The default rel is 1e-09 and abs_tol is 0.
Lesson: Comparisons and the trouble with floats
Machine epsilon
ε = 2−52 ≈ 2.22 × 10−16
The gap between 1.0 and the next float. sys.float_info.epsilon.
Lesson: Comparisons and the trouble with floats
Bitwise notExam favourite
~x = −x − 1
Python ints act like two's complement numbers with endless bits.
Lesson: Bitwise operators
ShiftsExam favourite
x << k = x · 2k, x >> k = x // 2k
Shifting is a fast way to multiply or divide by powers of 2.
Lesson: Bitwise operators
Useful tricks
x & 1 (odd?), x & (x − 1) == 0 (power of 2?), x ^ x == 0
Used in LeetCode problems such as Single Number and Power of Two.
Lesson: Bitwise operators
Euclidean style division in PythonExam favourite
a = q · b + r, q = ⌊a/b⌋, 0 ≤ r < b (b > 0)
For b < 0, b < r ≤ 0.
Lesson: The maths behind the operators
Last digit and dropping itExam favourite
n % 10, n // 10
Used to loop over the digits of a number.
Lesson: The maths behind the operators
Sum of digits test for 9
n % 9 == digit_sum(n) % 9
Because 10 % 9 = 1, every place value leaves remainder 1.
Lesson: The maths behind the operators
Float spacing near x
ulp(x) ≈ |x| · 2−52
math.ulp(x). Bigger numbers have bigger gaps between floats.
Lesson: The maths behind the operators

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    A unary operator has one operand (-x, not x, ~x). A binary operator has two (a + b). The same symbol - can be either.Lesson: Operators: the verbs of a program
  • In the exam
    C and Java cut integer division towards zero, so -7 / 2 is -3 there. Python floors, so -7 // 2 is -4. Exams love this difference.Lesson: Arithmetic: the seven number operators
  • Common mistake
    -2 ** 2 is -4, not 4. The power is done first, then the minus. Write (-2) ** 2 when you mean minus two squared.Lesson: Which operation goes first
  • In the exam
    not has a higher priority than and, and and is higher than or. So True or False and False is True or (False and False) = True.Lesson: Logical operators and short circuit
  • Common mistake
    "5" + 5 is a TypeError. Python never turns a number into text by itself. Use str(5) or an f-string.Lesson: Text operators and assignment shortcuts
1.4

Input, output and formatting text

Open chapter

input() and conversion, split and map, f-strings, the format spec, tables, older formatting, safe input.

Key ideas

  • input() Shows a prompt, waits, returns text. Convert with int() or float(). a, b = map(int, input().split()).
  • f-strings f"{expr}", {x!r}, {x = }, {x:spec}. {{ and }} for real brackets.
  • Format spec [[fill]align][sign][#][0][width][grouping][.precision][type]. Width is a minimum. .2f rounds half to even.
  • Older formatting "%s %d" % (a, b) and "{} {}".format(a, b). Prefer f-strings.
  • Safe input while True + try int(text) except ValueError + range check + break.

Formulas

Format spec grammarExam favourite
[[fill]align][sign][#][0][width][grouping][.precision][type]
Every part is optional, but the order is fixed. align is < > ^ or =.
Lesson: The format spec: width, alignment, decimals and more
Common types
d (int), f (fixed), e (scientific), % (percent), b o x X (bases), s (text)
No type means the same as str() for most values.
Lesson: The format spec: width, alignment, decimals and more
Padding added by a widthExam favourite
pad = max(0, width − len(text))
Width is a minimum. It never cuts the text.
Lesson: The maths: widths and rounding
Centre alignmentExam favourite
left = ⌊pad / 2⌋, right = pad − left
With an odd pad the extra character goes on the right.
Lesson: The maths: widths and rounding
Rounding to p places
round half to even on the exact binary value
f"{0.125:.2f}" is 0.12 because 0.125 is exact and 2 is even.
Lesson: The maths: widths and rounding
Digits of a number
len(str(n)) = ⌊log10 n⌋ + 1
For a whole number n > 0.
Lesson: The maths: widths and rounding

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    The Run button above feeds the typed answers (Asha and 25) for you. On your own computer, Python waits for you to type them.Lesson: Input and output: how a program talks to people
  • Common mistake
    input() returns text even when the user types digits. "5" + "5" is "55". Convert first, then calculate.Lesson: input() always returns text
  • Remember
    Since Python 3.12 (PEP 701) you may reuse the same quotes inside an f-string expression, for example f"{", ".join(names)}". Older versions need the other kind of quote inside.Lesson: f-strings: the modern way to build text
  • In the exam
    .2f rounds the stored binary value, and exact halves go to the even digit: f"{2.5:.0f}" gives 2 and f"{2.675:.2f}" gives 2.67.Lesson: The format spec: width, alignment, decimals and more
  • Remember
    Loops arrive in Core 2.2 and try/except in Core 5.1. You can use this pattern now and understand every line later.Lesson: Reading input safely

Step 2Core Python · Control flow

2.1

Making decisions: if, elif, else and match

Open chapter

if, elif, else, truthiness, combining conditions, conditional expression, walrus, match and case, De Morgan.

Key ideas

  • Chains if, any number of elif, optional else. First truthy condition wins, the rest are skipped. Strictest test first.
  • Truthiness Falsy: False, None, 0, 0.0, "", empty collections. "0" and [0] are truthy.
  • Combining and, or, not, 13 <= x <= 19, x in (a, b). x == a or b is always truthy.
  • One liners a if cond else b. (n := len(x)) assigns inside an expression.
  • match Literal, capture, _, |, [a, *rest], {"k": v}, Class(), guard if. A bare name captures.

Formulas

Conditional expressionExam favourite
value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
An expression, so it gives a value: kind = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd".
Lesson: One line choices: the conditional expression and the walrus
Assignment expression (walrus)
(name := expression)
Python 3.8+. Assigns and gives the value in one go, useful inside if and while conditions.
Lesson: One line choices: the conditional expression and the walrus
De Morgan lawsExam favourite
not (a and b) == (not a) or (not b), not (a or b) == (not a) and (not b)
Use them to simplify or flip a condition.
Lesson: The maths: boolean algebra
Number of pathsExam favourite
k independent if statements give up to 2k combinations
An elif chain with k conditions and an else has exactly k + 1 paths.
Lesson: The maths: boolean algebra
Distributive law
a and (b or c) == (a and b) or (a and c)
Like a × (b + c) = ab + ac in school algebra.
Lesson: The maths: boolean algebra

Tables

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Write if items: instead of if len(items) > 0:, and if not name: instead of if name == "":. PEP 8 recommends this short form. But write if x is None: when you really mean None, because 0 and "" are falsy too.Lesson: Truthy and falsy values
  • Common mistake
    if day == "Sat" or "Sun": is always True. Python reads it as (day == "Sat") or "Sun", and "Sun" is truthy. Write day in ("Sat", "Sun").Lesson: Combining conditions
  • Remember
    Do not chain many conditional expressions in one line. a if x else b if y else c is legal but hard to read. Use an if, elif, else statement instead.Lesson: One line choices: the conditional expression and the walrus
  • Common mistake
    A plain name in a case is a capture, not a comparison. case RED: catches everything and binds it to RED. To compare with a constant, use a dotted name such as case Color.RED:.Lesson: match and case: pattern matching
2.2

Loops: while, for, range, break and continue

Open chapter

while, for, range, break, continue, pass, loop else, loop patterns, nested loops, enumerate and zip, loop maths.

Key ideas

  • while and for while repeats while a condition is True. for repeats once per item of an iterable.
  • range range(start, stop, step) excludes stop. len = max(0, ceil((stop - start)/step)). step 0 is an error.
  • Loop control break leaves, continue skips, pass does nothing, loop else runs when no break happened.
  • Patterns Accumulator, counter, running max, search with break, build a list. Nested loops: outer x inner turns.
  • Pythonic loops enumerate(items, start=1), zip(a, b) stops at the shortest, reversed(), sorted().

Formulas

range(start, stop, step)Exam favourite
start, start + step, start + 2·step, ... while still before stop
stop is never included. start defaults to 0, step to 1. step must not be 0.
Lesson: for loops and range()
How many numbers range givesExam favourite
len = max(0, ⌈(stop − start) / step⌉)
range(1, 10, 3) has ⌈9/3⌉ = 3 numbers: 1, 4, 7.
Lesson: for loops and range()
Turns of a nested loopExam favourite
outer × inner
3 rows × 5 columns = 15 prints. Three nested loops of n each run n3 times.
Lesson: Loops inside loops
Triangle loopExam favourite
1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2
When the inner loop runs i times on turn i, the total is a triangular number.
Lesson: Loops inside loops
Length of a rangeExam favourite
len(range(a, b, s)) = max(0, ⌈(b − a)/s⌉)
Works for negative steps too: range(10, 0, -3) has ⌈-10/-3⌉ = 4 numbers.
Lesson: The maths of loops
Last number of a range
a + (len − 1) · s
range(0, 100, 7)[-1] = 0 + 14 × 7 = 98.
Lesson: The maths of loops
Sum of an arithmetic sequenceExam favourite
S = n(first + last)/2
sum(range(1, 101)) = 100 × 101 / 2 = 5050 (the young Gauss story).
Lesson: The maths of loops
Turns to halve n down to 1
⌊log2 n⌋
while n > 1: n //= 2 runs about log2 n times. This is why binary search is fast.
Lesson: The maths of loops
Digits of n (turns of the digit loop)
⌊log10 n⌋ + 1
The digit loop above ran 5 times for 90731.
Lesson: The maths of loops

Tables

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    range(5) is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: five numbers, but 5 itself is not included. This "stop is excluded" rule matches list indexes, so range(len(items)) gives every valid index.Lesson: for loops and range()
  • In the exam
    The loop else is not "else if the loop did not run". It means "no break happened". A for loop over an empty list runs its else block.Lesson: break, continue, pass and else
  • Remember
    Learn the loops first, then the shortcuts. In an interview you may be asked to write max() yourself, and the running maximum pattern is the answer.Lesson: Loop patterns every programmer uses
  • Common mistake
    break only leaves the inner loop. To leave two loops at once, put them in a function and use return, or set a flag and check it in the outer loop.Lesson: Loops inside loops
  • Common mistake
    zip stops at the shortest list. zip([1, 2, 3], "ab") gives only two pairs. Python 3.10 added zip(..., strict=True) to raise an error when the lengths differ.Lesson: enumerate, zip, reversed and sorted
  • Remember
    An infinite loop is not always a bug: servers and games run while True: with a break or return inside. In the REPL or a terminal, press Ctrl+C to stop a runaway loop.Lesson: When to use while

Step 3Core Python · Data collections

3.1

Strings: text, slicing, methods and Unicode

Open chapter

str, quotes, escapes, indexing, slicing, immutability, methods, split and join, Unicode, UTF-8, string maths.

Key ideas

  • Making strings Quotes: single, double or triple. Escapes start with a backslash. r"..." is a raw string. len() counts characters.
  • Index and slice s[0] first, s[-1] last. s[a:b:c] includes a, excludes b. s[::-1] reverses. Slices never raise IndexError.
  • Immutable You cannot change a character. Methods return new strings: write s = s.upper().
  • Key methods strip, split, join, replace, find (-1) vs index (ValueError), count, startswith, isdigit, isalpha, upper, lower.
  • Unicode ord("A") = 65, chr(97) = "a". UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per character. Compare strings by code point.

Formulas

Index of a characterExam favourite
0, 1, ..., len(s) − 1 from the left, and −1, −2, ..., −len(s) from the right
s[-k] is the same as s[len(s) − k].
Lesson: Indexing and slicing
SliceExam favourite
s[start:stop:step]
start is included, stop is not. Leave out start for "from the beginning" and stop for "to the end".
Lesson: Indexing and slicing
Length of a simple slice
len(s[a:b]) = b − a
when 0 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ len(s). "PYTHON"[1:4] is "YTH", 3 characters.
Lesson: Indexing and slicing
Number of substrings of a text of length nExam favourite
n(n + 1) / 2
Pick a start and an end. "abc" has 6: a, b, c, ab, bc, abc.
Lesson: The maths of strings
Number of subsequences (keep or drop each letter)
2n
Including the empty one. "abc" has 8.
Lesson: The maths of strings
Number of different arrangements (anagrams)Exam favourite
n! / (c1! · c2! · ...)
ci is how often each letter repeats. "banana": 6! / (3! · 2! · 1!) = 60.
Lesson: The maths of strings
Caesar shift of a lower case letter
new = (ord(ch) − 97 + k) mod 26 + 97
mod 26 wraps z round to a.
Lesson: The maths of strings
Polynomial hash of a text (used in Rabin Karp search)
h = (c0·bn−1 + c1·bn−2 + ... + cn−1) mod m
Lets a program compare a window of text with a pattern in O(1) by sliding the hash one letter at a time.
Lesson: The maths of strings

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Single and double quotes make exactly the same string. Pick one style and keep it. Use the other kind when the text itself contains a quote.Lesson: What a string is
  • In the exam
    A backslash starts an escape sequence: the backslash and the next character together stand for one special character. That is why len of the new line escape is 1. In a raw string (r before the quote) Python keeps every backslash, which is handy for Windows paths and regular expressions (Advanced 6.1).Lesson: Escape characters and raw strings
  • In the exam
    A single index outside the string raises IndexError. A slice outside the string never fails: it just gives what is there, or an empty string.Lesson: Indexing and slicing
  • Common mistake
    Strings are compared letter by letter by code point, not by dictionary order. All upper case letters (65 to 90) come before all lower case letters (97 to 122), so "Zebra" < "apple" is True. "10" < "9" is True too, because "1" comes before "9". Turn text into numbers before comparing numbers.Lesson: Joining, repeating, searching and comparing
  • Common mistake
    Every method returns a new string. s.upper() alone on a line does nothing useful. Write s = s.upper() to keep the result.Lesson: The most used string methods
  • In the exam
    split() with no argument and split(" ") are different. "a b".split() gives ["a", "b"], but "a b".split(" ") gives ["a", "", "b"] because there are two spaces.Lesson: split and join
  • Remember
    Most text problems follow one plan: walk through the characters with for ch in text, test each one (isalpha, isdigit, a comparison), and collect or count the ones you want. The Caesar cipher above uses ord() and chr() to do arithmetic on letters.Lesson: Working through text with loops
  • Common mistake
    Always say the encoding when you open a text file: open(name, encoding="utf-8"). Otherwise Python uses the system default, which is not UTF-8 on every Windows computer (Core 5.3).Lesson: Unicode, code points and UTF-8
3.2

Lists: storing, changing, sorting and copying

Open chapter

list methods, sort vs sorted, aliases and copies, matrices, bubble sort, unpacking, list growth and costs.

Key ideas

  • Lists Ordered, changeable, any types. Index from 0, slice like strings. len, min, max, sum, in.
  • Add and remove append (one item), extend (many), insert(i, x). remove(x) first match, pop() last, pop(i), del items[i].
  • Sorting sort() changes the list and returns None. sorted() returns a new list. key= and reverse=. Stable.
  • Copies b = a is the same list. a[:] or a.copy() is a shallow copy. copy.deepcopy for nested lists. [[0]*n for _ in range(m)].
  • Costs append, pop(), index access O(1). insert(0), pop(0), in, remove O(n). Bubble sort n(n-1)/2 comparisons.

Formulas

Item of a matrixExam favourite
matrix[row][col]
The first index picks the row, the second the column.
Lesson: Lists in lists: matrices
Transpose
T[c][r] = M[r][c]
An r × c matrix becomes c × r.
Lesson: Lists in lists: matrices
Number of items
rows × cols
A 3D list (a cube) has rows × cols × depth items.
Lesson: Lists in lists: matrices
Comparisons in the worst caseExam favourite
(n − 1) + (n − 2) + ... + 1 = n(n − 1)/2
5 items need at most 10 comparisons, 1,000 items about 500,000. That is O(n2).
Lesson: Bubble sort, step by step
Best case with the early stop
n − 1 comparisons
An already sorted list needs one pass.
Lesson: Bubble sort, step by step
Average cost of an append (amortised)Exam favourite
(n + total copies) / n < a small constant
With growth by a factor g > 1 the copies form a geometric series n/g + n/g2 + ... < n/(g − 1).
Lesson: The maths of lists
Bubble sort comparisonsExam favourite
n(n − 1)/2
The same sum as the triangle loop of Core 2.2.
Lesson: The maths of lists
Number of slices items[a:b] with a < b
C(n + 1, 2) = n(n + 1)/2
Choose 2 of the n + 1 cut points.
Lesson: The maths of lists
Mean of a list
sum(items) / len(items)
Undefined for an empty list: guard against ZeroDivisionError.
Lesson: The maths of lists

⌊log2 n⌋ + 1
A sorted list of 1,000,000 items needs at most 20 checks with bisect (Advanced 4.2).

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    append adds one item, even if that item is a list. [1, 2].append([3, 4]) gives [1, 2, [3, 4]]. extend adds the items one by one and gives [1, 2, 3, 4].Lesson: Adding and changing items
  • Common mistake
    Do not remove items from a list while a for loop is walking over it. The loop skips the item after each removal. Loop over a copy (for x in items[:]) or build a new list instead.Lesson: Removing items
  • Remember
    x in items checks each item from the left until it finds a match, so it takes O(n) time. For many lookups in a big collection use a set or a dict (Core 3.3 and 3.4), which answer in O(1) on average.Lesson: Finding items
  • In the exam
    [[0] * 3] * 3 makes one inner list and three references to it, so changing one row changes all three. Build a grid with a comprehension: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)].Lesson: Shallow copy, deep copy and lists of lists
  • Remember
    Never use bubble sort in real code. sorted() is far faster. Learn it to understand sorting and to answer exam questions.Lesson: Bubble sort, step by step
  • In the exam
    The number of names must match the number of items, unless one name has a star. a, b = [1, 2, 3] raises ValueError: too many values to unpack.Lesson: Unpacking, swapping and a first look at comprehensions
  • Remember
    pop(0) and insert(0, x) move every other item. For a queue that adds at one end and removes at the other, use collections.deque, which does both in O(1) (Advanced 4.2).Lesson: Lists compared with other collections
3.3

Tuples and sets: fixed records and unique items

Open chapter

tuples, packing and unpacking, hashable keys, namedtuple, sets, set algebra, deduplication, O(1) membership, set maths.

Key ideas

  • Tuples Immutable ordered sequence. (5,) is a tuple, (5) is not. count and index only. Unpack with a, b = t.
  • Hashable Dict keys and set items must be hashable: numbers, strings, tuples of hashables, frozensets. Not lists, sets or dicts.
  • Sets Unique items, no order. set() is empty. add, remove (KeyError), discard (safe), pop (any item).
  • Set algebra | union, & intersection, - difference, ^ symmetric difference, <= subset. Methods accept any iterable.
  • Counting |A u B| = |A| + |B| - |A n B|. A set of n items has 2^n subsets. x in set is O(1) on average.

Formulas

Size of a union (inclusion and exclusion)Exam favourite
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|
The middle part was counted twice, so take it away once.
Lesson: The maths of sets
Three sets
|A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|
Add singles, take away pairs, add back the triple.
Lesson: The maths of sets
Symmetric difference
|A Δ B| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B|
A ^ B in Python.
Lesson: The maths of sets
Number of subsets (the power set)Exam favourite
2n
Each item is in or out. {1, 2, 3} has 8 subsets.
Lesson: The maths of sets
De Morgan's laws
not (A or B) = (not A) and (not B)
For sets inside a universe U: U − (A ∪ B) = (U − A) ∩ (U − B).
Lesson: The maths of sets

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    The comma makes a tuple, not the brackets. (5) is the number 5. (5,) is a tuple with one item. This is a favourite exam trick.Lesson: Making and using tuples
  • Common mistake
    A tuple holds references. You cannot change which objects it holds, but if one of them is a list, that list can still change. Such a tuple is not hashable, so it cannot be a dict key.Lesson: What "cannot change" means
  • Remember
    A named tuple gives each position a name, so p.x is clearer than p[0]. For records with many fields or that need to change, use a dataclass (Advanced 1.3).Lesson: Tuples as keys, and named tuples
  • In the exam
    {} is an empty dict, not an empty set. Write set() for an empty set. Also, a set can only hold hashable items: numbers, strings, tuples of them, but not lists or other sets.Lesson: Making sets and changing them
  • In the exam
    The operators need two sets. The methods accept any iterable, so A.union([1, 2]) works but A | [1, 2] raises TypeError.Lesson: Union, intersection, difference
  • Remember
    set(items) is the fastest way to remove repeats, but the order is lost. If order matters, use list(dict.fromkeys(items)), which keeps the first time each item appears.Lesson: Removing duplicates
  • Remember
    A frozenset is a set that cannot change. Because it never changes it is hashable, so it can be a dict key or an item of another set.Lesson: frozenset and set comprehensions
3.4

Dictionaries: keys, values and hash tables

Open chapter

dict basics, get and setdefault, keys values items, counting, grouping, nesting and JSON, merging, hash table internals.

Key ideas

  • Dicts Key to value mapping. Keys unique and hashable, values anything. Ordered by insertion since 3.7.
  • Read safely d[k] raises KeyError. d.get(k, default) does not. k in d checks keys only.
  • Change d[k] = v adds or replaces. del d[k], d.pop(k, default), d.popitem() (last added), update, |, |=.
  • Loop for k in d (keys), d.values(), d.items(). Do not add or remove keys while looping, use list(d).
  • Patterns Count: d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1 or Counter. Group: dict of lists or defaultdict(list). Two Sum: dict of seen values.

Formulas

Slot of a keyExam favourite
slot = hash(key) mod table size
Table sizes are powers of 2, so this is just the last few bits of the hash.
Lesson: The maths of hashing
Load factorExam favourite
α = used slots / table size ≤ 2/3
A CPython dict with 8 slots holds at most 5 keys. The 6th key makes it grow.
Lesson: The maths of hashing
New table size
smallest power of 2 ≥ 3 × (number of keys)
When the 6th key arrives, 5 keys are stored: 3 × 5 = 15, so the new size is 16.
Lesson: The maths of hashing
Expected probes for a lookup that hits (uniform hashing)
about (1/α) ln(1/(1 − α))
At α = 2/3 this is about 1.6 probes, so lookups stay fast.
Lesson: The maths of hashing
Chance that two of k keys share a slot of m (birthday problem)
1 − e−k(k − 1)/(2m)
With 23 people and 365 days the chance of a shared birthday is above 50 percent. Collisions are normal, so tables must handle them.
Lesson: The maths of hashing

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    for x in d gives the keys, not the values and not the pairs. Use d.values() for values and d.items() for (key, value) pairs. x in d also checks keys only.Lesson: Looping over a dict
  • Common mistake
    keys(), values() and items() return views: windows onto the dict that update by themselves. Adding or removing keys while you loop over a dict raises RuntimeError. Loop over list(d) instead.Lesson: Views, and changing a dict while looping
  • Remember
    Counting is the most common use of a dict. Learn the get(word, 0) + 1 line by heart, then use collections.Counter in real code. Counter also adds, subtracts and finds the most common items.Lesson: Counting with a dict
  • Remember
    A dict of dicts and lists looks exactly like JSON, the text format that web APIs use. json.dumps turns a dict into JSON text and json.loads turns it back. The web part of this subject uses this all the time.Lesson: Nested dicts and JSON
  • Common mistake
    dict.fromkeys(keys, []) gives every key the same list object. Appending to one changes all of them. Use a comprehension {k: [] for k in keys} instead.Lesson: Merging, comprehensions and other ways to build
  • In the exam
    Keys are compared with ==. Because 1 == 1.0 == True and they have the same hash, they are the same key: the dict keeps the first key object and the last value. Use one type for your keys.Lesson: What can be a key

Step 4Core Python · Functions

4.1

Functions: def, return and every kind of argument

Open chapter

def, return, None, argument kinds, *args, **kwargs, / and *, unpacking, mutable defaults, docstrings, first-class functions.

Key ideas

  • def and return def name(params): body. return value leaves the function. No return gives None. print is not return.
  • Argument kinds Positional by order, keyword by name, positional before keyword. Defaults make parameters optional.
  • Star parameters *args tuple of extra positionals, **kwargs dict of extra keywords. Bare * means keyword-only after it, / means positional-only before it.
  • Mutable default Defaults are made once at def time. Use None, then create the list inside.
  • Functions are objects Assign them, store them, pass them: sorted(key=f), map(f, items). Docstring on the first line, type hints are not enforced.

Formulas

A function maps each input to one outputExam favourite
f: X → Y, x ↦ f(x)
area(width, height) maps each pair of numbers to one number.
Lesson: Functions in maths and in code
CompositionExam favourite
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))
apply_twice(f, x) is f(f(x)). len(str(n)) is len ∘ str.
Lesson: Functions in maths and in code
Idempotent function
f(f(x)) = f(x)
abs, str.strip and sorted are idempotent: doing them twice changes nothing more.
Lesson: Functions in maths and in code
How many functions from a set of m inputs to n outputs
nm
Each of the m inputs can go to any of the n outputs. From {1, 2, 3} to {a, b}: 23 = 8.
Lesson: Functions in maths and in code
Arguments a call may give with p positional parameters, d of them with defaults and no *args
between p − d and p positional arguments
describe has p = 3, d = 1, so 2 or 3 positional arguments.
Lesson: Functions in maths and in code

Lesson: return, print and None

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    A parameter is the name in the def line (name, width). An argument is the value you pass in the call ("Asha", 4). Exams use both words, so learn the difference.Lesson: What a function is
  • In the exam
    A function with no return, or with a bare return, gives back None. That is why a = show_double(5) printed 10 but left a as None.Lesson: return, print and None
  • In the exam
    describe(name="Sara", 25) is a SyntaxError: a positional argument may not follow a keyword argument. Python refuses to even start the program.Lesson: Positional, keyword and default arguments
  • Remember
    The full order is: positional-only, /, normal, *args (or a bare *), keyword-only, **kwargs. The names args and kwargs are only a habit. What matters is the * and **.Lesson: *args, **kwargs, keyword-only and positional-only
  • In the exam
    In a def line, * and ** collect arguments. In a call, * and ** spread a list or dict out into separate arguments. Same symbols, opposite jobs.Lesson: Spreading lists and dicts into a call
  • Remember
    A docstring is a string on the first line of the body. help(bmi) and editors show it. Type hints such as height_m: float and -> float tell readers and tools like mypy what you expect, but Python itself does not check them when the program runs (Advanced 3.1).Lesson: Docstrings and type hints
  • Remember
    A function name is just a variable that holds a function object. You can give it another name, store it in a list or dict, and pass it to another function. Functions that take or return functions are called higher-order functions. Core 4.3 uses this with sorted, map, filter and closures.Lesson: Functions are objects too
4.2

Scope and recursion: LEGB, closures and the call stack

Open chapter

scope, LEGB, global, nonlocal, closures, recursion, call stack, recursion limit, memoisation, recurrences.

Key ideas

  • Scopes Local (inside a call), Enclosing, Global (module), Built-in: LEGB. Assigning makes a name local in the whole function.
  • global and nonlocal global x assigns the module x. nonlocal x assigns the enclosing function x. Reading needs neither.
  • Closures An inner function that remembers enclosing names (cells). Used for counters, factories and decorators.
  • Recursion Base case + smaller recursive case. Each call is a frame. Limit about 1000, RecursionError.
  • Costs T(n) = T(n-1) + c is O(n). Naive fib 2F(n+1) - 1 calls, lru_cache makes it n + 1. Hanoi 2^n - 1. Fast power O(log n).

Formulas

Recurrence for a simple recursionExam favourite
T(n) = T(n − 1) + c gives T(n) = O(n)
factorial and countdown do constant work and then one smaller call.
Lesson: The maths of recursion
Calls made by naive fib(n)Exam favourite
C(n) = C(n − 1) + C(n − 2) + 1 = 2F(n + 1) − 1
fib(5) makes 2 × 8 − 1 = 15 calls, as the animation counts.
Lesson: The maths of recursion
Golden ratio growth
F(n) ≈ φn / √5, φ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618
So naive fib is exponential: about 1.6n calls.
Lesson: The maths of recursion
Tower of Hanoi movesExam favourite
M(n) = 2M(n − 1) + 1 = 2n − 1
3 discs need 7 moves, 64 discs need about 1.8 × 1019.
Lesson: The maths of recursion
Fast power
T(n) = T(n/2) + c gives T(n) = O(log n)
power(2, 1000) needs only about 10 levels of calls.
Lesson: The maths of recursion
Master theorem (divide and conquer)
T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(nd)
If d > logb a: O(nd). If equal: O(nd log n). If less: O(nlogb a). Merge sort: a = 2, b = 2, d = 1 gives O(n log n).
Lesson: The maths of recursion

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    Assigning to a name inside a function makes a new local name, even if a global with the same name exists. This is called shadowing. Changing an object (items.append) is different from rebinding a name (items = [...]): the first is seen by the caller, the second is not.Lesson: Local names hide global names
  • In the exam
    Python decides which names are local when it compiles the function, not while it runs. If a name is assigned anywhere in the function, it is local in the whole function.Lesson: The LEGB rule
  • Remember
    The fix is either to rename the local variable, to pass count in as a parameter, or, if you really mean the global, to add global count at the top of the function.Lesson: UnboundLocalError
  • In the exam
    global reaches the module scope. nonlocal reaches the nearest enclosing function scope and is a SyntaxError at the top level. Decorators (Advanced 1.2) are built from closures.Lesson: nonlocal and closures
  • Common mistake
    Each call uses a frame on the call stack. To protect the program, CPython stops at about 1,000 frames deep with RecursionError. sys.setrecursionlimit can raise the limit, but a recursion that deep is usually better written as a loop.Lesson: The recursion limit
  • Remember
    total(items[1:]) is clear but copies the list each time, which makes it O(n2). Real code uses sum(). Fast power is the opposite: halving the exponent makes it O(log n), which is how pow(a, b, m) handles huge numbers in cryptography.Lesson: Classic recursive functions
4.3

lambda, map, filter and comprehensions

Open chapter

lambda, key functions, map, filter, reduce, list, dict and set comprehensions, generator expressions, higher-order functions.

Key ideas

  • lambda lambda args: expression. One expression, no statements. Best as an argument, def otherwise.
  • key functions sorted/min/max(items, key=f). Tuple keys sort by several fields. -x reverses a number key.
  • map, filter, reduce Lazy iterators: list(map(f, a)), list(filter(test, a)). functools.reduce(f, a, start) folds to one value.
  • Comprehensions [expr for x in a if test], [a if t else b for x in s], {k: v for ...}, {x for ...}. Outer for first.
  • Generator expressions (expr for x in a): lazy, one use, tiny memory. sum(x*x for x in a), any(...), all(...).

Formulas

List comprehensionExam favourite
[expression for item in iterable if condition]
Read it as: the expression, for each item, but only if the condition holds.
Lesson: List comprehensions
With if-elseExam favourite
[a if test else b for item in iterable]
The if-else is part of the expression, so it comes before for. A filter if comes after.
Lesson: List comprehensions
Set builder notationExam favourite
{ f(x) | x ∈ S, p(x) }
Maths wrote "the set of f(x) for x in S where p(x)" long before Python. {f(x) for x in S if p(x)} is the same idea.
Lesson: The maths behind comprehensions
map is f applied to each item
map(f, [a1, ..., an]) = [f(a1), ..., f(an)]
The length does not change.
Lesson: The maths behind comprehensions
reduce is a foldExam favourite
reduce(⊕, [a1, a2, a3], s) = ((s ⊕ a1) ⊕ a2) ⊕ a3
With + this is the sum, with max it is the maximum.
Lesson: The maths behind comprehensions
Size of a comprehension with two for clauses
|A| × |B|
[(x, y) for x in range(1, 4) for y in "ab"] has 3 × 2 = 6 pairs, the Cartesian product A × B.
Lesson: The maths behind comprehensions
Sum of squares
12 + 22 + ... + n2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
sum(n * n for n in range(1, 11)) = 10 × 11 × 21 / 6 = 385.
Lesson: The maths behind comprehensions

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    A lambda cannot contain statements such as if blocks, for loops, return or assignment with =. It can contain a conditional expression: lambda n: "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd".Lesson: lambda: a function in one expression
  • Remember
    key is a function that is called once per item. Python sorts by what it returns. To sort by two things, return a tuple: tuples compare item by item. To reverse just one of two numeric keys, make it negative.Lesson: Sorting and choosing with key
  • Common mistake
    map and filter return iterators, not lists. They give each value once, only when asked. Wrap them in list() to see all the values, and do not loop over the same map object twice.Lesson: map, filter and reduce
  • In the exam
    [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0 else 0] is a SyntaxError. An if after for only filters and has no else.Lesson: List comprehensions
  • Remember
    In [v for row in matrix for v in row] the for clauses are in the same order as nested loops: outer first. A comprehension inside the expression ([[... for c] for r]) builds a list of lists. If it needs more than two for clauses, a normal loop is easier to read.Lesson: Nested comprehensions
  • Remember
    A higher-order function takes a function or returns one: sorted, map, filter, make_greeter, compose and partial are all examples. functools.partial is often clearer than a lambda that only fixes some arguments.Lesson: Higher-order functions, compose and partial

Step 5Core Python · Errors, modules and files

5.1

Exceptions: try, except, else, finally and raise

Open chapter

try, except, else, finally, exception hierarchy, propagation, raise, custom exceptions, assert, EAFP, with.

Key ideas

  • try and except try: risky code. except X as err: handles X and its children. First matching handler only.
  • else and finally else runs if no exception. finally always runs (cleanup). Order: try, except..., else, finally.
  • Hierarchy BaseException > Exception > ArithmeticError > ZeroDivisionError. LookupError > KeyError, IndexError. KeyboardInterrupt is not an Exception.
  • raise raise ValueError("msg"). Bare raise re-raises. raise New() from err sets __cause__. Custom: class MyError(Exception).
  • Style Catch specific classes, never bare except. assert is for programmer checks (-O removes it). EAFP. with closes resources.

Formulas

Handlers checked before a matchExam favourite
position of the first matching except clause
Python stops at the first match, so order decides the cost and the meaning.
Lesson: Counting and reasoning about failures
Chance that at least one of n independent steps failsExam favourite
1 − (1 − p)n
With p = 1 percent per network call, 50 calls fail at least once with chance 1 − 0.9950 ≈ 39 percent. Errors are normal at scale, so handle them.
Lesson: Counting and reasoning about failures
Expected tries until success (retry loop)
1 / q
If each try succeeds with chance q = 0.8, you need 1.25 tries on average (a geometric distribution).
Lesson: Counting and reasoning about failures
Exponential back off before retry k
wait = base × 2k
1, 2, 4, 8 seconds. Used by web clients so a busy server is not flooded (Web 2.2).
Lesson: Counting and reasoning about failures

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Read a traceback from the bottom up. The last line names the exception and the reason. The lines above show where it happened, with the newest call last. Python 3.11 and later mark the exact part of the line with ^ and ~ characters.Lesson: When things go wrong: exceptions
  • Common mistake
    Avoid a bare except: or except BaseException:. They also catch KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, so Ctrl+C stops working. Catch Exception at most, and only where you log or report the error.Lesson: The exception hierarchy and the order of handlers
  • In the exam
    The order is fixed: try, then except clauses, then else, then finally. You need at least one except or a finally. else keeps code out of the try block, so you do not accidentally catch errors from it.Lesson: else and finally
  • Remember
    A low level function often cannot know what the right reaction is. average should not print "No marks yet" because it may be used in a web page or a report. Let it raise, and handle the exception at the level that knows what to tell the user. This is called delegating responsibility.Lesson: Exceptions travel up through function calls
  • Remember
    Make your own exceptions by subclassing Exception (never BaseException). Give your program one base class, such as BankError, and make specific errors its children. Callers can then catch one exact problem or every problem of your program. Classes are explained in Core 6.1.Lesson: Your own exception classes
  • Remember
    A with statement uses a context manager that closes the file (or releases a lock, or ends a database transaction) even when an exception happens. It is the short, safe form of try and finally. Advanced 2.2 shows how to write your own.Lesson: Cleaning up: finally and with
5.2

Modules and packages: import, the standard library and pip

Open chapter

import forms, sys.modules and sys.path, math, random, platform, own modules and packages, __all__, main guard, pip and venv.

Key ideas

  • import forms import m, import m as a, from m import x, from m import x as y. Avoid import *. Relative: from . import x.
  • How import works Check sys.modules, search sys.path, run the file once, cache it, bind the name. importlib.reload re-runs.
  • math and random ceil, floor, trunc, sqrt, isqrt, hypot, factorial, comb, gcd, log, isclose. randint(a, b) includes b, randrange excludes stop, seed repeats.
  • Packages Folder + __init__.py. _name is private by convention. __all__ controls import *. __pycache__ holds .pyc files.
  • Main guard and pip if __name__ == "__main__": main(). pip install inside a venv. pip freeze > requirements.txt.

Formulas

Combinations and permutationsExam favourite
C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!), P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!
math.comb(5, 2) = 10, math.perm(5, 2) = 20.
Lesson: Maths you get from math and random
Euclid: greatest common divisorExam favourite
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), gcd(a, 0) = a
gcd(84, 36) = gcd(36, 12) = gcd(12, 0) = 12. lcm(a, b) = a × b / gcd(a, b).
Lesson: Maths you get from math and random
Change of base for logarithms
logb x = ln x / ln b
math.log(8, 2) = 3.0. Floats can make this 2.9999999999999996 for other numbers, so use log2 for base 2.
Lesson: Maths you get from math and random
Expected value of a fair die (randint(1, 6))
E = (1 + 2 + ... + 6)/6 = 3.5
The mean of many rolls gets close to 3.5 (law of large numbers).
Lesson: Maths you get from math and random
Monte Carlo estimate of π
π ≈ 4 × (points with x2 + y2 ≤ 1) / (all points)
Random points in a square, counted inside a quarter circle. The error shrinks like 1/√n.
Lesson: Maths you get from math and random

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    floor goes down and trunc goes toward zero. They agree for positive numbers and differ for negative ones: floor(−4.8) is −5, trunc(−4.8) is −4. round() is a built-in, not in math, and rounds halves to the even number.Lesson: The math module
  • Common mistake
    random gives pseudo-random numbers from the Mersenne Twister algorithm: good for games and simulations, but predictable. For passwords, tokens and anything secret use the secrets module (secrets.token_hex(16)).Lesson: The random module
  • Remember
    The output above came from the build machine. Press Run on this page and platform.system() says Emscripten, because the Python on this page runs inside your browser (Pyodide). The same code gives Windows or Darwin on other computers.Lesson: platform and sys: where am I running
  • Common mistake
    Any file name.py that Python can find is a module called name. Use lower case names with underscores, and never name your file after a standard module: a file called random.py in your folder hides the real random module, and import random gives you your own file.Lesson: Writing your own module
  • Remember
    Since Python 3.3 a folder without __init__.py can still be imported as a namespace package, but an __init__.py makes the intent clear and lets you run setup code and choose what the package exports.Lesson: Packages: folders of modules
  • Remember
    Run pip as python -m pip install ... when you are not sure which Python a plain pip belongs to. Modern projects describe their dependencies in a pyproject.toml file, and tools such as uv and poetry manage environments for you.Lesson: pip, PyPI and virtual environments
5.3

Files: reading, writing, modes, paths and streams

Open chapter

open modes, with, read and write methods, binary files, encodings, errno, pathlib, os and shutil, streams, csv and json.

Key ideas

  • open and with with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as f: closes automatically. Modes r, w (empties), a, x (new only), +, b.
  • Reading read(), read(n), readline() ("" at end), readlines(), for line in f (best for big files). Lines keep their new line.
  • Writing write(s) and writelines(list) add no new lines. print(x, file=f) does. write returns characters written.
  • Binary and cursor "rb"/"wb" use bytes. bytearray + readinto. seek(n) moves, tell() reports.
  • Errors and paths OSError family: FileNotFoundError (ENOENT), FileExistsError, PermissionError. pathlib.Path / "x", glob, read_text.

Formulas

File size in bytes of an ASCII textExam favourite
sum of len(line) for all lines, new lines included
"milk\n" is 5 bytes. On Windows a text file stores each new line as 2 bytes (\r\n).
Lesson: Sizes, bytes and cursors
UTF-8 sizeExam favourite
1 byte for code points 0 to 127, 2 up to 2,047, 3 up to 65,535, 4 above
"नमस्ते ₹100 café\n" has 16 characters but 31 bytes.
Lesson: Sizes, bytes and cursors
Units
1 KB = 1,000 bytes, 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes
Disks are sold in KB, MB, GB (powers of 10). Operating systems often show KiB, MiB, GiB (powers of 2).
Lesson: Sizes, bytes and cursors
Cursor after a read in text mode (ASCII)
new position = old position + characters read
In binary mode tell() is always a byte offset. In text mode it is an opaque number, so only seek() to values that tell() gave you.
Lesson: Sizes, bytes and cursors
Lines in memory
readlines(): O(file size). for line in f: O(longest line)
A 10 GB log can be processed with a for loop on a laptop with 8 GB of memory.
Lesson: Sizes, bytes and cursors

1233Remove Sub-Folders from the FilesystemMediumSort, then compare with the last kept folderAfter sorting, a sub folder comes right after its parent. Keep a folder unless it starts with the last kept folder plus "/".
1047Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In StringEasyStackPush each character. If it equals the top of the stack, pop instead.
68Text JustificationHardGreedy lines, spread spacesFill each line with as many words as fit. Spread the spaces, giving the left gaps one extra when they do not divide evenly. The last line is left aligned.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    All the programs in this chapter first move into a new empty temporary folder with tempfile.mkdtemp(), so they never touch your own files. Drop that line when you work in your project folder.Lesson: Files: data that lasts
  • In the exam
    Lines keep their new line character. Use line.strip() or line.rstrip("\n") before you compare or split them. For big files loop with for line in f, which reads one line at a time instead of loading gigabytes into memory.Lesson: Reading a text file
  • Common mistake
    Add t (text, the default) or b (binary) to any mode: "rb", "wb", "ab", "r+b". The most common accident is opening a file with "w" when you meant "a": the old contents are gone at once.Lesson: Open modes
  • Common mistake
    Without encoding=..., open() uses a default that depends on the computer. It is UTF-8 on Linux and macOS but can be an old code page on Windows, so a file written on one computer may not read on another. Since Python 3.15 the default becomes UTF-8 everywhere (PEP 686), but writing encoding="utf-8" is still the safe habit.Lesson: Encodings: always say utf-8
  • Common mistake
    os.remove, os.rename and shutil.rmtree do not use a recycle bin: deleted files are gone. Print the paths and check them before you delete anything in a loop.Lesson: Folders with os and shutil
  • Remember
    The page shows only stdout, so the stderr line above is not in the output. In a terminal both appear, but they are separate streams: python3 app.py > out.txt saves only stdout and still shows errors on the screen.Lesson: stdin, stdout and stderr
  • Common mistake
    Never split CSV lines with line.split(","). A value like "Ravi, Jr" contains a comma and is stored in quotes. The csv module handles quotes, commas and new lines inside values correctly. Advanced 6.2 covers csv, json, xml and sqlite3 in depth.Lesson: CSV and JSON files

Step 6Core Python · Object oriented programming

6.1

Classes and objects: attributes, methods, self and encapsulation

Open chapter

classes, objects, __init__, self, instance and class attributes, __str__ and __repr__, introspection, name mangling, is and ==.

Key ideas

  • Class and object class C: defines a blueprint. C(...) makes an object and runs __init__(self, ...). self is the object.
  • Two kinds of attribute self.x is per object (in obj.__dict__). x = ... in the class body is shared. Read looks in the object, then the class. Write goes to the object.
  • Shared list trap A list or dict class attribute is shared by all objects. Create it in __init__.
  • Text forms __str__ for print and str, __repr__ for repr, lists and debugging. Write __repr__ at least.
  • Introspection and privacy type, isinstance, hasattr, getattr, setattr, vars, __name__, __module__, __bases__. _x is a convention, __x becomes _Class__x. is = same object.

Formulas

Length of a vector (Pythagoras)Exam favourite
|v| = √(x2 + y2)
Vector(3, 4).length() is √(9 + 16) = 5.
Lesson: The maths inside a class
Dot productExam favourite
a · b = axbx + ayby
(3, 4) · (1, 2) = 3 + 8 = 11.
Lesson: The maths inside a class
Angle between two vectors
cos θ = (a · b) / (|a| |b|)
cos θ = 11 / (5 × 2.236) = 0.984, so θ = 10.3 degrees.
Lesson: The maths inside a class
Counting objects with a class attribute
count after n objects = n
One class attribute is shared, so 3 students give Student.count = 3.
Lesson: The maths inside a class
Name mangling
__name inside class C becomes _C__name
__balance in Account becomes _Account__balance (17 characters).
Lesson: The maths inside a class
Memory
n objects store n copies of each instance attribute but 1 copy of each class attribute and method
1,000 dogs: 1,000 names, 1 species, 1 bark function.
Lesson: The maths inside a class

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    self is not a keyword. It is only the name every Python programmer uses for the first parameter of a method. Python fills it in for you: rex.bark() becomes Dog.bark(rex). Forget self in the def line and the call fails with "takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given".Lesson: Methods, self and __init__
  • In the exam
    Writing obj.attr = value never goes to the class. It always creates or changes the attribute on that one object. That is why a.species = "wolf" left b.species and Dog.species alone.Lesson: Instance attributes and class attributes
  • Common mistake
    A class attribute that holds a list, dict or set is ONE object for all instances. Changing it with append or update through any object changes it for every object. Create such data in __init__ with self.items = [] instead. This is the same trap as a mutable default argument (4.1).Lesson: The shared list trap
  • In the exam
    Inside a method, change a class attribute through the class name: Student.count += 1. Writing self.count += 1 reads the class value but then stores the result on the object, so the class counter would never change.Lesson: Class attributes as counters
  • Remember
    getattr with a name in a variable is how frameworks such as Django read a field whose name comes from a settings file or a URL.Lesson: Introspection: looking inside objects
  • In the exam
    Encapsulation means an object guards its own data and offers methods to work with it, so outside code cannot put it into a bad state (like a negative balance). Python trusts programmers: it has no real private keyword like Java. Use one underscore for internal things, and properties (Advanced 1.3) when you need checks on reading or writing.Lesson: Encapsulation, _private and name mangling
  • In the exam
    a is b asks "are these the same object". a == b asks "are these equal". For your own classes == means the same as is until you write __eq__. Writing __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, so the objects can no longer be set items or dict keys unless you also write __hash__ (Advanced 1.1).Lesson: Identity and equality of objects
  • Remember
    Each method keeps the object valid: deposit refuses amounts that are not positive and withdraw refuses to go below zero. Code outside the class never has to repeat these checks. That is the main gain of object oriented design.Lesson: Putting it together: a bank account
6.2

Inheritance: super(), overriding, polymorphism and the MRO

Open chapter

inheritance, overriding, super(), isinstance, polymorphism, duck typing, abstract methods, mixins, MRO, composition.

Key ideas

  • Inherit and override class Child(Parent): reuses Parent. Writing a method again overrides it. Lookup: object, class, then parents in MRO order, ending at object.
  • super() super().__init__(...) runs parent setup. super().m() extends a method. super() means the next class in the MRO of the object.
  • Checks isinstance counts children, type(x) is C does not. issubclass(bool, int) is True. __bases__ and __mro__ show the family.
  • Polymorphism One call works on many types. Duck typing needs only the method. Abstract methods: NotImplementedError or abc with @abstractmethod.
  • MRO and composition C3: child before parents, parents in written order, each once. Impossible order is TypeError. Prefer has a over is a.

Formulas

C3 linearisationExam favourite
L[C] = C + merge(L[B1], ..., L[Bn], [B1, ..., Bn])
B1 ... Bn are the parents of C in the order written.
Lesson: The MRO and the diamond problem
The merge rule
take the first head that is not in the tail of any list, remove it everywhere, repeat
If every head is in some tail, there is no valid order and Python raises TypeError.
Lesson: The MRO and the diamond problem
CircleExam favourite
A = πr2
Circle(2): 3.14159 × 4 = 12.57.
Lesson: The maths: areas, MROs and lookup cost
Heron for a triangleExam favourite
s = (a + b + c) / 2, A = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c))
Triangle(3, 4, 5): s = 6, A = √(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 6.
Lesson: The maths: areas, MROs and lookup cost
Total area by polymorphism
total = sum of shape.area() for every shape
12.57 + 12 + 6 = 30.57, one loop for every kind of shape.
Lesson: The maths: areas, MROs and lookup cost
Length of an MRO
len(C.__mro__) = number of distinct ancestors + 1 (C itself), object included
Diamond D(B, C): D, B, C, A, object is 5.
Lesson: The maths: areas, MROs and lookup cost
Lookup cost
worst case one dict check per class in the MRO: O(len(MRO))
CPython caches the result per type, so repeated lookups are close to O(1).
Lesson: The maths: areas, MROs and lookup cost

284Peeking IteratorMediumWrap an object and look one step aheadKeep the next value in an attribute. peek returns it, next returns it and fetches a new one. This is composition: the class holds another object.
341Flatten Nested List IteratorMediumFlatten once with recursionWalk the nested list with a recursive helper and store every integer in a plain list. Then next and hasNext only move an index.

Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    The child is a special kind of the parent: a Dog is an Animal. If you cannot say "a Child is a Parent" in plain words, inheritance is probably the wrong tool (see composition below).Lesson: Inheritance: reuse a class
  • In the exam
    An overriding method normally keeps the same parameters as the parent one, so code that works with an Animal also works with a Dog. This rule is called the Liskov substitution principle.Lesson: Overriding methods
  • Common mistake
    A child __init__ replaces the parent one completely. If it does not call super().__init__(...), the attributes the parent sets are never created.Lesson: super(): use the parent version
  • In the exam
    Prefer isinstance over type(x) == C, because a child object is also a valid parent object. Every class inherits from object in the end, and bool is a child of int, which is why True + True is 2.Lesson: isinstance, issubclass and __bases__
  • Remember
    A mixin is a small class that adds one ability (like to_json) and is not meant to be used alone. Django uses mixins a lot, for example LoginRequiredMixin on views. Put mixins first or last consistently and keep them free of __init__ when you can.Lesson: Multiple inheritance and mixins
  • In the exam
    super() does not mean "my parent". It means "the next class in the MRO of the object I am working on". Inside B, super().hello() went to C for a D object but to A for a B object. That is what lets every class in a diamond run exactly once.Lesson: The MRO and the diamond problem

Step 7Core Python · Exam practice

7.1

Exam practice: PCEP and PCAP style papers

Open chapter

Four practice papers, a bug hunt, the traps table, exam technique and a mock quiz.

Key ideas

  • Exam facts PCEP-30-02: 30 questions, 40 min, 70 %. PCAP-31-03: 40 questions, 65 min, 70 %. OOP is 34 % of PCAP.
  • Operator traps -2 ** 2 is -4, 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, -7 // 2 is -4, -7 % 3 is 2, round(2.5) is 2, 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.
  • Collection traps b = a aliases, [[0] * 3] * 3 shares a row, (1,) is a tuple, {} is a dict, sort returns None.
  • Function traps Mutable defaults are shared, assignment makes a name local, lambdas in loops bind late, finally always runs.
  • Object traps obj.x = v never changes the class, __x becomes _Class__x, a child __init__ must call super().__init__().

Step 1Advanced Python · Advanced object oriented programming

1.1

Special methods and operator overloading

Open chapter

special methods, operator overloading, reflected operators, total_ordering, the hash contract, container protocol, __call__, __format__.

Key ideas

  • How operators work a + b calls type(a).__add__(a, b). Missing or NotImplemented: try type(b).__radd__(b, a), then TypeError. Lookup is on the class.
  • Text __repr__ (developers, lists, REPL), __str__ (print), __format__ (f-string specs).
  • Compare and hash __eq__ plus __lt__ with total_ordering. Equal objects need equal hashes. __eq__ alone makes a class unhashable.
  • Containers __len__, __getitem__ (ints and slices), __setitem__, __contains__, __iter__. __bool__ falls back to __len__.
  • Other hooks __call__ for callable objects, __iadd__ returns self, __getattr__ only on failed lookup, __setattr__ on every assignment.

Formulas

Adding fractionsExam favourite
a/b + c/d = (ad + cb) / bd
1/2 + 1/3 = (3 + 2) / 6 = 5/6.
Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators
Lowest termsExam favourite
divide top and bottom by g = gcd(top, bottom)
2/4: gcd(2, 4) = 2, so 1/2.
Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators
Euclid
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), gcd(a, 0) = a
gcd(48, 18) = gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6) = gcd(6, 0) = 6.
Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators
Vector length
|v| = √(x2 + y2)
abs(Vector(3, 4)) = 5.0, using math.hypot.
Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators
Scaling
k(x, y) = (kx, ky)
2 * Vector(3, 4) = Vector(6, 8), through __rmul__.
Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators
Dot product with @
a @ b = axbx + ayby
Python 3.5 added @ (__matmul__) for exactly this kind of product.
Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    Special methods are looked up on the class, not on the object. Setting obj.__len__ = ... on one object does nothing for len(obj). Also, never invent your own __names__: they are reserved for Python.Lesson: The main special methods
  • In the exam
    Return the special value NotImplemented (not raise NotImplementedError) when your method cannot handle the other type. That gives the other object a chance to answer. Raising stops Python from trying.Lesson: Arithmetic, reflected and unary operators
  • Remember
    If you write __eq__ but not __ne__, Python gives != for free by inverting __eq__.Lesson: Comparisons and total_ordering
  • Remember
    A class with only __len__ and __getitem__ already works with for, in, reversed and slicing. That is why Python calls this the sequence protocol. Inheriting from collections.abc.Sequence (or MutableSequence) also gives you index, count and more for free.Lesson: Emulating containers
  • In the exam
    x += y first tries x.__iadd__(y) and then ASSIGNS the result to x. That is why __iadd__ must return self. A tuple has no __iadd__, so += makes a new tuple and other names still see the old one.Lesson: Callable objects, text formats and in place operators
  • Remember
    0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 with floats, but Fraction(1, 10) + Fraction(2, 10) is exactly 3/10. Use Fraction or Decimal when exact answers matter, such as money.Lesson: The maths: fractions and vectors with operators
1.2

Extended arguments, closures and decorators

Open chapter

parameters, closures, decorators, wraps, decorator factories, stacking, class decorators, cache.

Key ideas

  • Parameters a, / positional only. *args tuple. after * keyword only. **kwargs dict. f(*seq, **d) unpacks at a call.
  • Closures Functions are objects. An inner function remembers the variables of the outer one (__closure__), even after it returned.
  • Decorator shape @d def f is f = d(f). def d(func): @wraps(func) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): ... return func(*args, **kwargs). return wrapper.
  • Arguments and stacking @d(x) is f = d(x)(f): three levels. @a @b def f is a(b(f)): applied bottom up, run top down.
  • Built ins @cache, @lru_cache(maxsize), @wraps, @property, @classmethod, @staticmethod, @dataclass, @contextmanager. Cache only pure functions.

Formulas

Calls of plain recursive FibonacciExam favourite
C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2), C(0) = C(1) = 1, so C(n) = 2F(n + 1) − 1
fib(25): 2 × 121,393 − 1 = 242,785 calls, as the program counted.
Lesson: The maths: memoisation and backoff
Calls with @cacheExam favourite
each n from 0 to N is computed once: N + 1 misses
fib(25): 26 misses and 23 hits.
Lesson: The maths: memoisation and backoff
Growth
F(n) ≈ φn / √5, φ = (1 + √5) / 2 ≈ 1.618
Plain recursion is exponential, O(φn). The cached version is linear, O(n).
Lesson: The maths: memoisation and backoff
Exponential backoff
wait before retry k = base × 2k, total for n retries = base(2n − 1)
base 1 s, 4 retries: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 s.
Lesson: The maths: memoisation and backoff
LRU hit rate
hit rate = hits / (hits + misses)
square with maxsize 2 on 1, 2, 1, 3, 2: 1 hit, 4 misses, 20 %.
Lesson: The maths: memoisation and backoff

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    The order in a def is always: positional only, /, normal, *args (or a bare *), keyword only, **kwargs. *args, **kwargs in a wrapper accept any call and pass it on unchanged, which is why every general decorator uses them. Notice the fourth line of output: name="Asha" did not fill name. Because describe has **extra, it went into extra, so Python reports name as missing.Lesson: Extended argument syntax
  • Remember
    A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the function it was made in, even after that function has returned. greet remembers greeting. That memory, stored in __closure__, is what lets a wrapper keep hold of the original function.Lesson: Functions are objects, closures remember
  • Common mistake
    Without @wraps every decorated function is called "wrapper" and loses its docstring, which breaks help(), debuggers, logging and frameworks that look up functions by name (Flask uses the name for its routes). Always put @wraps(func) on the wrapper.Lesson: functools.wraps: keep the name and docstring
  • Common mistake
    A decorator with arguments has three nested functions: the factory (settings), the decorator (the function) and the wrapper (the call). Forgetting the brackets, @retry instead of @retry(3), passes the function as attempts and fails in a confusing way.Lesson: Decorators with arguments
  • In the exam
    Decorators are applied from the bottom up (nearest the def first) and run from the top down at call time. @a then @b above def f means f = a(b(f)).Lesson: Stacking decorators
  • Common mistake
    Only cache pure functions, whose result depends only on the arguments. Arguments must be hashable. @cache never forgets, so for many different arguments use lru_cache with a maxsize.Lesson: Built in decorators and caching
1.3

Class design: methods, properties, abstract classes and dataclasses

Open chapter

class and static methods, properties, cached_property, ABCs, dataclasses, __slots__, descriptors.

Key ideas

  • Method kinds Instance method gets self. @classmethod gets cls (alternative constructors, returns cls(...)). @staticmethod gets nothing.
  • Properties @property getter, @x.setter with checks, no setter means read only. Store the value as self._x. @cached_property computes once.
  • Abstract classes class C(ABC) with @abstractmethod: C() and incomplete children raise TypeError. collections.abc offers ready contracts.
  • Dataclasses @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__, __eq__. field(default_factory=list), frozen, order, __post_init__, kw_only, slots, asdict, replace.
  • Slots and descriptors __slots__ removes __dict__. Descriptors have __get__ and __set__. Data descriptors beat the instance dict.

Formulas

Celsius to Fahrenheit (a computed property)Exam favourite
F = C × 9 / 5 + 32
25 °C is 25 × 1.8 + 32 = 77 °F.
Lesson: The maths: conversions, ordering and memory
The other way
C = (F − 32) × 5 / 9
212 °F is 180 × 5 / 9 = 100 °C.
Lesson: The maths: conversions, ordering and memory
Absolute zero
C ≥ −273.15, so F ≥ −459.67
The setter rejects anything colder.
Lesson: The maths: conversions, ordering and memory
order=True compares as tuplesExam favourite
(a1, a2, ...) < (b1, b2, ...) at the first position where they differ
Version(3, 9, 7) < Version(3, 14, 0) because 9 < 14, even though "9" > "14" as text.
Lesson: The maths: conversions, ordering and memory
Memory for n objects
total ≈ n × bytes per object
1,000,000 objects at 40 bytes less each save about 40 MB.
Lesson: The maths: conversions, ordering and memory
Age from a birth year (ignoring the birthday)
age = current year − birth year
2026 − 1996 = 30.
Lesson: The maths: conversions, ordering and memory

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    Student.from_text returned a Student because the method calls cls(...), not Person(...). That is why alternative constructors should be class methods.Lesson: Instance, class and static methods
  • Common mistake
    Store the real value under another name (self._celsius). If the setter wrote self.celsius = value it would call itself forever and raise RecursionError.Lesson: Properties: attributes with rules
  • Remember
    An abstract base class is a contract: "every Payment can pay and has a name". Python refuses to create an object until every abstract method is filled in, so a forgotten method fails at once instead of in front of a customer. collections.abc gives ready made contracts like Sized, Iterable, Sequence and Mapping.Lesson: Abstract base classes
  • Remember
    __slots__ removes the per object __dict__, so objects are smaller and adding a misspelt attribute fails at once. In Python 3.14 a normal object already keeps its attributes compactly until you touch __dict__, so the saving is smaller than older guides say: about a third in this run. Use slots for classes with very many objects.Lesson: __slots__ and descriptors
  • In the exam
    A descriptor is an object with __get__, __set__ or __delete__, stored as a class attribute. property, classmethod, staticmethod and every normal method are descriptors. Write your own when the same rule (like "must be positive") applies to many attributes in many classes.Lesson: __slots__ and descriptors
1.4

Exceptions in depth, copying and serialisation

Open chapter

exception hierarchies, chaining, tracebacks, notes, exception groups, warnings, shallow and deep copy, pickle and shelve.

Key ideas

  • Exception design class AppError(Exception) plus children. super().__init__(message). Catch the child for one problem, the base for all.
  • Chaining raise New() from err sets __cause__. Raising inside except sets __context__. from None hides it. err.__traceback__ has the frames.
  • 3.11 tools err.add_note(text) and err.__notes__. ExceptionGroup(msg, [errors]) caught with except* Type.
  • Copies b = a no copy. a.copy(), a[:], list(a), dict(a), copy.copy: shallow. copy.deepcopy: everything, loops handled by memo.
  • Saving objects pickle.dumps/loads (bytes), dump/load (files in "wb"/"rb"). Never unpickle untrusted data. shelve: dict on disk, returns copies.

Formulas

Chance that k independent attempts all failExam favourite
P(all fail) = pk, P(success) = 1 − pk
A call fails 20 % of the time. With 3 attempts: 1 − 0.23 = 99.2 % success.
Lesson: The maths: retries, copies and sizes
Objects created by copies of an n by m nested listExam favourite
shallow: 1 list. deep: 1 + n lists
For [[1, 2], [3, 4]]: shallow makes 1 new list, deep makes 3. The ints are immutable and shared either way.
Lesson: The maths: retries, copies and sizes
Attempts needed for a target
k ≥ log(1 − target) / log(p)
p = 0.2, target 99.99 %: k ≥ log(0.0001) / log(0.2) ≈ 5.7, so 6 attempts.
Lesson: The maths: retries, copies and sizes
Expected attempts until success
E = 1 / (1 − p)
p = 0.2: 1.25 attempts on average.
Lesson: The maths: retries, copies and sizes

331Verify Preorder Serialization of a Binary TreeMediumCount open slotsStart with one slot. Every token fills a slot, and a number opens two more. The string is valid if slots never go below zero and end at zero.
652Find Duplicate SubtreesMediumSerialise every subtreeTurn each subtree into a string (its own little pickle). Count the strings and report a root the second time its string appears.
394Decode StringMediumA stack of unfinished partsRead the text once. A number before [ says how many times to repeat. On [ save the text so far and the count on a stack. On ] repeat the inner text and glue it to the saved text. This is how a loader rebuilds nested data from a flat string.
1106Parsing A Boolean ExpressionHardA stack of values and operatorsPush every character except commas. On ) pop the values back to the (, take the operator in front of it, and push the single result. Nested expressions are solved from the inside out.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Give your package one base exception (ShopError) and children for each problem. Callers can then catch one specific error, or everything from your package with one except.Lesson: Exceptions, copies and saved objects
  • In the exam
    Use raise ... from err when you turn a low level error into a meaningful one, so the original is never lost. Use from None only when the original adds nothing for the reader.Lesson: Chaining: __cause__ and __context__
  • Common mistake
    Never unpickle data from a source you do not trust. pickle.loads can run any code the data asks for, so a crafted file can take over your computer. For data from users or the internet use JSON.Lesson: pickle and shelve: save objects
  • In the exam
    A shelf returns copies. db["ravi"]["tags"].append("work") changes a copy that is thrown away. Read the value, change it and assign it back (or open with writeback=True).Lesson: pickle and shelve: save objects
1.5

Metaprogramming: type, class hooks and metaclasses

Open chapter

classes as objects, type(), introspection, __init_subclass__, class decorators, metaclasses, creation order.

Key ideas

  • Classes are objects type(x) gives the class. type(Dog) is the metaclass (normally type). type(type) is type. Classes can be stored, passed and returned.
  • type() with three arguments type(name, bases, namespace) builds a class. A class statement does the same. The body runs once and fills the namespace.
  • Introspection getattr(obj, name, default), setattr, hasattr, delattr, callable, vars, dir, __class__, __bases__, __mro__, __subclasses__(), inspect.signature.
  • Hooks __init_subclass__ on the parent runs for every child (registries, checks). Class decorators get the finished class.
  • Metaclasses class Meta(type): __new__ builds the class, __call__ makes objects. Inherited by children. Conflicts raise TypeError. Prefer lighter tools.

Formulas

Classes made by a factory
classes = n1 × n2 × ... × nk
make_record for 3 colours and 4 sizes builds 3 × 4 = 12 classes.
Lesson: The maths: counting classes, lookups and steps
Classes in a full hierarchy below one baseExam favourite
b + b2 + ... + bd = b(bd − 1) / (b − 1)
With b = 3 children each and d = 2 levels: 3 + 9 = 12 subclasses, each one seen by __init_subclass__.
Lesson: The maths: counting classes, lookups and steps
Average checks in an if and elif chainExam favourite
average = (n + 1) / 2 for n equally likely names
A chain of 9 actions needs 5 checks on average. A dict or getattr needs about 1 lookup.
Lesson: The maths: counting classes, lookups and steps
Worst case attribute lookup
dicts checked ≤ 1 + len(C.__mro__)
The instance dict, then each class in the MRO. For Kitten, Cat, object: at most 1 + 3 = 4.
Lesson: The maths: counting classes, lookups and steps
Objects made by a singleton
objects = 1 for any n ≥ 1 calls, against n for a normal class
50 calls of Config() make 1 object.
Lesson: The maths: counting classes, lookups and steps
Steps from an object up to type
type(rex) = Dog, type(Dog) = Meta, type(Meta) = type, type(type) = type
Three steps reach type, and then the chain repeats itself.
Lesson: The maths: counting classes, lookups and steps
