Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    type has two jobs. With one argument, type(x) tells you the class of x. With three arguments, type(name, bases, namespace) builds a new class. And type(type) is type: type is its own class, which is where the chain ends.Lesson: Classes are objects too
  • Remember
    A class statement and a type() call give exactly the same kind of class. Python itself turns every class statement into a call like type("Cat", (object,), namespace). You only need type() directly when the name or the fields are known only while the program runs, for example from a config file.Lesson: Building classes with type()
  • Common mistake
    The class body runs once, at the moment Python reaches the class statement, not each time you make an object. Names it creates (tax, price, total) end up in the namespace dict, which becomes the class __dict__. That is why a class body can hold any normal code, even print.Lesson: Building classes with type()
  • In the exam
    __init_subclass__ (PEP 487, Python 3.6) runs on the PARENT every time a child class is created. It is a class method automatically. Keyword arguments in the class line, like name="csv", are passed to it. Always call super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs) so other parents in a multiple inheritance chain get their turn.Lesson: __init_subclass__ and class decorators
  • Remember
    A class decorator is a function that takes a finished class and returns a class, usually the same one after changing it. @dataclass, @functools.total_ordering and @enum.unique are class decorators from the standard library. Stacked decorators run from the bottom up, so auto_repr ran before route.Lesson: __init_subclass__ and class decorators
  • In the exam
    A metaclass is a subclass of type. Its __new__(mcs, name, bases, namespace) gets everything the class statement collected and must return the new class, normally from super().__new__. Children of Job use CheckMeta too, because Python uses the metaclass of the base class when none is given. The check fires when the class is DEFINED, long before anyone uses it.Lesson: Metaclasses
  • Common mistake
    Calling a class, Config(...), really calls type(Config).__call__. The normal type.__call__ runs __new__ and then __init__. Overriding __call__ in a metaclass changes what calling the class does: here it returns the saved object. Notice that the second call did not even run __init__, so mode stayed "prod".Lesson: Metaclasses
  • Remember
    You already use metaclasses: ABC is built by ABCMeta (that is how abstract methods block objects) and every Enum by EnumType (that is why len(Colour) and for c in Colour work on the class itself). A class whose bases have two unrelated metaclasses cannot be made, because Python cannot pick one metaclass that is a child of both.Lesson: Metaclasses

Step 2Advanced Python · Iterators, generators and context managers

2.1

Iterators and generators

Open chapter

iterator protocol, iterator classes, yield, pipelines, yield from, send, throw, close, lazy built ins.

Key ideas

  • Iterator protocol iter(x) gives an iterator. next(it) gives a value or raises StopIteration. next(it, default) avoids the error. A for loop does this for you.
  • Iterable versus iterator Iterables (list, range, dict) give a fresh iterator each time. Iterators (zip, map, files, generators) are used up after one pass.
  • Generators A function with yield returns a generator. Nothing runs until next(). It pauses at each yield and keeps its locals. Return ends it.
  • Pipelines and laziness Chain generators: values are made only when asked, memory stays constant, and islice or break stops work early.
  • Advanced control yield from delegates and returns the inner return value. send(v), throw(e), close() (GeneratorExit). Prime with next() before send.

Formulas

Memory of a list against a generatorExam favourite
list: about 8n bytes of pointers plus the items, generator: a constant (about 200 bytes)
100,000 squares: the list needs about 800 KB of pointers, the generator stays near 200 bytes.
Lesson: The maths: memory, early stopping and counting
Work done by a lazy searchExam favourite
items read = position of the first match (k), not n
Looking for the first even square above 50 in 1, 2, 3, ... reads 8 numbers and stops (8 × 8 = 64).
Lesson: The maths: memory, early stopping and counting
Running average after k values
averagek = (x1 + x2 + ... + xk) / k
After 10, 20 and 60: (10 + 20 + 60) / 3 = 30.
Lesson: The maths: memory, early stopping and counting
Number of next() calls to see StopIteration
values + 1
countdown(4) gives 4 values, and the 5th call raises StopIteration.
Lesson: The maths: memory, early stopping and counting
Subsets and combinations (LeetCode 77 and 90)
subsets = 2n, combinations of k from n = n! / (k! (n − k)!)
From 5 numbers choose 2: 5! / (2! × 3!) = 10.
Lesson: The maths: memory, early stopping and counting
A pipeline of s stages over n items
time grows with n × s, memory with s only
106 lines through 4 stages: 4 × 106 stage steps, but only 4 paused generators in memory.
Lesson: The maths: memory, early stopping and counting

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    iter(nums) gave a NEW iterator each time, so the first answer was False. An iterator returns itself from iter(), so the second was True. That is the whole difference: an iterable can make many iterators, an iterator is one walk that can be used once.Lesson: Iterators and generators: one value at a time
  • Common mistake
    Raising StopIteration ends the loop. Do not raise it inside a generator body: since Python 3.7 (PEP 479) it is turned into RuntimeError. In a generator, simply return.Lesson: Writing iterators as classes
  • In the exam
    A function that contains yield anywhere is a generator function. Calling it runs nothing: the first line, print("start"), only ran at the first next(). After the last value the generator is closed, and list() on a used generator gives an empty list.Lesson: Generator functions and yield
  • Remember
    Building the pipeline read nothing. Asking for 2 errors read only 4 lines and never touched "WARN slow" or the last line. Each value travels through all three stages before the next line is read. Unix pipes such as grep | cut | head work the same way.Lesson: Generator pipelines
  • Remember
    yield from other passes every value of other straight to whoever is asking, and when other finishes, its return value becomes the value of the yield from expression. It is the clean way to split a big generator into smaller ones, and it handles send and throw for you too.Lesson: yield from, send, throw and close
  • Common mistake
    A common bug: saving map(...) or zip(...) in a variable, looping over it once for a check, and then finding it empty the second time. Wrap it in list(...) if you need it twice.Lesson: Lazy tools you already use
2.2

itertools, functools and operator

Open chapter

endless iterators, slicing, joining, groupby, combinatorics with formulas, reduce, partial, singledispatch, operator.

Key ideas

  • Endless and slicing count, cycle, repeat never stop: use islice, zip, takewhile. takewhile/dropwhile cut at the first failure. compress applies a mask.
  • Joining chain, chain.from_iterable, zip_longest(fillvalue=), pairwise, batched, starmap, accumulate(func, initial=), tee.
  • groupby Joins neighbours with equal keys only. Sort by the same key first. Use each group before moving on.
  • Combinatorics product n**r, permutations n!/(n-r)!, combinations C(n,r), with replacement C(n+r-1,r). math.comb and math.perm count without listing.
  • functools and operator reduce (left fold), partial, singledispatch, lru_cache and cache_info. itemgetter, attrgetter, methodcaller as key functions.

Formulas

product(items, repeat=r)Exam favourite
nr
3 items, r = 2: 32 = 9 tuples.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds
permutations(items, r)Exam favourite
P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!
4 items, r = 2: 24 / 2 = 12.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds
combinations(items, r)Exam favourite
C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n − r)!)
4 items, r = 2: 24 / (2 × 2) = 6.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds
combinations_with_replacement(items, r)
C(n + r − 1, r)
3 items, r = 2: C(4, 2) = 6.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds
Pascal's rule
C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r)
C(4, 2) = C(3, 1) + C(3, 2) = 3 + 3 = 6: tuples with the first item, plus tuples without it.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds
Prefix sums with accumulateExam favourite
P = accumulate(a, initial=0), sum of a[i] to a[j] = P[j + 1] − P[i]
a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], P = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14], a[1] + a[2] + a[3] = 9 − 3 = 6.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds
reduce is a left fold
reduce(f, [a, b, c]) = f(f(a, b), c)
reduce(operator.sub, [10, 3, 2]) = (10 − 3) − 2 = 5.
Lesson: The maths: counting, prefix sums and folds

Tips and traps

  • Common mistake
    count, cycle and repeat never end on their own. Always stop them: with islice, zip with something finite, takewhile, or a break.Lesson: The iterator toolbox
  • Remember
    tee keeps every value that one copy has seen and the other has not, so if one copy runs far ahead it can use as much memory as a list. Use it when both copies move at a similar pace.Lesson: Joining, pairing and running totals
  • Common mistake
    groupby only joins items that are NEXT to each other. On unsorted data tea appeared twice. Sort by the same key first, or use a dict (collections.defaultdict(list)) when you cannot sort.Lesson: groupby: runs of equal keys
  • In the exam
    singledispatch chose the int version for 21, the list version for [1, 2] and the base version for 2.5. It looks at the type of the FIRST argument only. For methods use functools.singledispatchmethod.Lesson: functools: reduce, partial, singledispatch and caches
  • Remember
    lru_cache(maxsize=2) keeps the 2 most recently used answers. Calling 1, 2, 1, 3, 1 gave 2 hits: when 3 arrived, 2 was the least recently used and was thrown away.Lesson: functools: reduce, partial, singledispatch and caches
  • Remember
    The itertools documentation ends with a long list of recipes like these: sliding_window, unique_everseen, first_true, roundrobin, partition and more. The third party package more-itertools has all of them ready to install with pip.Lesson: Recipes built from the tools
2.3

Context managers and the with statement

Open chapter

with, __enter__ and __exit__, suppressing errors, @contextmanager, standard managers, exit order, ExitStack.

Key ideas

  • The with protocol with X as v: v = X.__enter__(), body, then X.__exit__(type, err, tb) always. Methods are looked up on the type.
  • Suppressing __exit__ returning True hides the exception. contextlib.suppress(Error) hides only the listed types.
  • @contextmanager Set up, then yield the as value inside try, then clean up in finally. Re raise errors you do not handle. Works as a decorator.
  • Standard managers open, Lock, TemporaryDirectory, chdir, redirect_stdout, localcontext, closing, nullcontext, sqlite3 (transaction), mock.patch.
  • Several managers Entered left to right, exited right to left. Bracketed form across lines. ExitStack: enter_context and callback for a dynamic number.

Formulas

Exit order of n nested managersExam favourite
the k-th one entered is the (n − k + 1)-th one exited
with A, B, C: A is entered 1st and exited 3rd.
Lesson: The maths: leaks, failures and exit order
Chance that at least one of n steps failsExam favourite
1 − (1 − p)n
Each of 10 steps fails with p = 0.01: 1 − 0.9910 ≈ 9.6 %. Errors are common, so clean up must not depend on success.
Lesson: The maths: leaks, failures and exit order
Expected leaks without with
leaks = calls × p (chance a path forgets to close)
1000 calls with p = 0.02 leak about 20 files. With with: 0.
Lesson: The maths: leaks, failures and exit order
Time until a leaking server runs out of file handles
requests = free handles / leaks per request
1024 handles and 2 leaks per request: 512 requests.
Lesson: The maths: leaks, failures and exit order
Elapsed time with a timer context manager
elapsed = texit − tenter
Entered at 1.50 s, exited at 2.75 s: 1.25 s.
Lesson: The maths: leaks, failures and exit order

No.ProblemLevelPatternHint
636Exclusive Time of FunctionsMediumA stack of running functionsLogs open and close like nested with blocks. Keep a stack of running ids. When something starts or ends, give the time since the last event to the function on top.
946Validate Stack SequencesMediumReplay the pushes and pops on a real stackPush each value. After every push, pop while the top is the next value that should come out. It works if the stack ends empty, just as every with block must close in reverse order.
921Minimum Add to Make Parentheses ValidMediumCount open bracketsTrack how many "(" are still open. A ")" with nothing open needs an added "(". At the end every open one needs a ")".
1249Minimum Remove to Make Valid ParenthesesMediumA stack of open positionsPush the index of each "(". A ")" with an empty stack is removed. Any "(" left on the stack at the end is removed too.
856Score of ParenthesesMediumA stack of scores per levelOpening starts a new level with score 0. Closing turns the level into 1 if it was empty, or double its score otherwise, and adds it to the level outside.
1190Reverse Substrings Between Each Pair of ParenthesesMediumA stack of unfinished textOn "(" save the text so far and start fresh. On ")" reverse the inner text and glue it to the saved text.
32Longest Valid ParenthesesHardA stack of indexes with a baseKeep the index of the last unmatched position at the bottom of the stack. After each match, the length is the current index minus the index on top.
735Asteroid CollisionMediumA stack of survivorsOnly a left moving asteroid can hit the right moving ones on the stack. Pop the smaller ones, stop if it is destroyed.
844Backspace String CompareEasyBuild each text with a stackPush letters, pop on "#". Compare the two results.
2390Removing Stars From a StringMediumA stack againEach star removes the closest letter on its left: push letters and pop on "*".
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    A file object is its own context manager: its __exit__ calls close(). Always open files with with. In CPython an unclosed file is usually closed by garbage collection, but other Pythons (PyPy) and long running programs can run out of file handles first.Lesson: Context managers and the with statement
  • Common mistake
    Only return True from __exit__ on purpose and only for the exact errors you expect. Hiding every error makes bugs invisible. contextlib.suppress(SomeError) is the clear, ready made way to say "this error is fine here".Lesson: Suppressing exceptions
  • In the exam
    Everything before yield is the set up, the yielded value goes into as, and everything after yield is the clean up. The try and finally around the yield is what makes the clean up run after an error: without it, an exception in the body would be raised at the yield and skip the rest.Lesson: contextmanager: a context manager from a generator
  • Remember
    nullcontext is handy when a with is sometimes needed and sometimes not: lock if threaded else nullcontext().Lesson: Context managers in the standard library
  • In the exam
    Managers are entered left to right and exited in the reverse order, like a stack: the last one opened is the first one closed. That is what you want: an inner resource that depends on an outer one is cleaned up first.Lesson: Several managers and ExitStack
  • Remember
    ExitStack is for when the number of managers is only known while the program runs. enter_context adds a manager, callback adds any function to call at the end, and everything is cleaned up in reverse order, even if opening the third file fails.Lesson: Several managers and ExitStack

Step 3Advanced Python · Professional code: style, testing and logging

3.1

Clean code: PEP 8, docstrings and type hints

Open chapter

Zen of Python, PEP 8 layout and names, bug preventing habits, docstrings, doctest, type hints, ruff, black, mypy.

Key ideas

  • PEP 8 layout 4 spaces, 79 characters, 2 blank lines around top level defs, imports one per line grouped stdlib, third party, local.
  • PEP 8 names snake_case functions and variables, CapWords classes, UPPER_CASE constants, _private by convention.
  • Bug preventing habits is None, if items:, isinstance, startswith and endswith, None instead of mutable defaults, small try blocks.
  • Docstrings PEP 257: """One line summary.""" then details. __doc__ and help() read it. doctest runs >>> examples.
  • Type hints and tools list[int], int | None, Callable, Protocol, TypedDict, Literal, Final, def f[T]. Not checked at run time: use mypy, ruff and black.

Formulas

Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe)Exam favourite
M = E − N + 2 (edges and nodes of the control flow graph) = decision points + 1
circle_area has one if, so M = 1 + 1 = 2. ruff rule C901 warns when M is above a limit, often 10.
Lesson: The maths: complexity, paths and line budgets
Paths through k independent if statementsExam favourite
paths = 2k
4 separate ifs give 16 paths. Smaller functions keep this testable.
Lesson: The maths: complexity, paths and line budgets
Minimum tests to cover every independent path
tests ≥ M
A function with M = 6 needs at least 6 tests for basis path coverage.
Lesson: The maths: complexity, paths and line budgets
Characters left on a line
room = 79 − indent
Code nested 2 levels deep (8 spaces) has 71 characters left.
Lesson: The maths: complexity, paths and line budgets
Spaces of indentation
spaces = 4 × depth
3 levels deep: 12 spaces. Deep nesting eats the line budget, a hint to split the function.
Lesson: The maths: complexity, paths and line budgets

Tables

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    The Zen is a set of values, not rules. Lines like "Readability counts", "Explicit is better than implicit" and "Errors should never pass silently" explain WHY PEP 8 and good habits exist.Lesson: Clean code: style, docstrings and type hints
  • In the exam
    black fixed the layout but not the names, the unused import or == None: a formatter only moves spaces and line breaks, it never changes meaning. That is why teams use a formatter AND a linter. ruff can do both (ruff format and ruff check).Lesson: PEP 8: layout and names
  • Remember
    PEP 8 also says: use isinstance instead of comparing types, use startswith and endswith instead of slicing, do not compare booleans to True with ==, and keep try blocks small so you only catch the error you expect.Lesson: Rules that prevent bugs
  • Remember
    doctest finds >>> lines in docstrings, runs them and compares the output with the next line. TestResults(failed=0, attempted=2) means both examples still work. It keeps documentation honest. Real test suites come in 3.2.Lesson: Docstrings and doctest (PEP 257)
  • In the exam
    Hints are stored in __annotations__ but Python never checks them while running: first("hello") worked although the hint says list. In Python 3.14 annotations are evaluated lazily (PEP 649 and 749), so a hint can even name a class defined later in the file.Lesson: Type hints
3.2

Testing: unittest, pytest and mocks

Open chapter

unittest, fixtures, failures and errors, mocks, pytest, coverage, property based testing, test strategy.

Key ideas

  • unittest class T(unittest.TestCase), methods test_..., assertEqual, assertTrue, assertIn, assertRaises (with), assertAlmostEqual, setUp, subTest, skip.
  • Outcomes PASSED, FAILED (assert false), ERROR (other exception). Read the last line. Tests must not depend on each other.
  • Mocks Mock().m.return_value, side_effect (list or exception), assert_called_once_with, call_count, patch and patch.object. Inject dependencies.
  • pytest test_ functions with plain assert, fixtures by parameter name, parametrize, approx, raises(match=), tmp_path, monkeypatch, -v, -k.
  • Strategy Edges and just outside, every fixed bug, coverage is not correctness, property tests with Hypothesis, the test pyramid, TDD.

Formulas

Line coverageExam favourite
coverage = lines run / total lines × 100 %
17 of 19 lines run: 17 / 19 ≈ 89.5 %.
Lesson: The maths: coverage, boundaries and binary search
Boundary value tests for a range a to bExam favourite
test a − 1, a, b, b + 1 (and one value inside)
percent from 0 to 100: test −1, 0, 100, 101 and 50, five tests.
Lesson: The maths: coverage, boundaries and binary search
Combinations of k options with v values each
all combinations = vk
3 settings with 4 values each: 64 tests. Pairwise testing covers every pair of values with far fewer, about v2 = 16.
Lesson: The maths: coverage, boundaries and binary search
Binary search steps (the LeetCode set)Exam favourite
steps ≤ ⌈log2(n + 1)⌉
n = 1000 sorted items: at most 10 steps. This is also how git bisect finds the commit that broke a test.
Lesson: The maths: coverage, boundaries and binary search
Chance a random test hits a bug that needs one value out of N
1 − (1 − 1/N)t after t tests
N = 1000 and t = 100: about 9.5 %. Picking edge cases on purpose beats random luck.
Lesson: The maths: coverage, boundaries and binary search

Table: no. · problem · level · pattern
No.ProblemLevelPatternHint
704Binary SearchEasyHalve the range each stepKeep low and high. Look at the middle. The famous bug is an off by one in the loop condition, so test arrays of length 0, 1 and 2.
35Search Insert PositionEasyBinary search for the first place not smallerWhen the loop ends, low is where target belongs. Test before the first item and after the last.
278First Bad VersionEasyBinary search on a yes or no questionExactly what git bisect does with a failing test. The is_bad check is passed in, so a test can give a fake one.
374Guess Number Higher or LowerEasyBinary search against an APIThe guess API answers -1, 1 or 0. In tests we inject a fake API, like a Mock with a side effect.
34Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted ArrayMediumTwo binary searchesFind the first index not smaller than target and the first index bigger than target. bisect_left and bisect_right do exactly this.
162Find Peak ElementMediumWalk uphill with binary searchIf the middle is lower than its right neighbour, a peak lies to the right. Otherwise it lies at the middle or to the left.
153Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted ArrayMediumCompare the middle with the right endIf the middle is bigger than the last item, the drop (and the minimum) is to the right.
33Search in Rotated Sorted ArrayMediumOne half is always sortedCheck which half is in order, then whether target lies inside it. Many edge cases: test a rotation at every position.
875Koko Eating BananasMediumBinary search on the answerTry a speed in the middle and count the hours needed. Too slow: go faster. Fast enough: try slower.
4Median of Two Sorted ArraysHardBinary search the cut in the shorter arrayCut both arrays so the left parts hold half of all items and every left item is at most every right item. Then the median comes from the four items around the cuts.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    unittest is built into Python. A test is a method whose name starts with test_ inside a class that inherits from unittest.TestCase. assertEqual, assertTrue, assertIn, assertRaises and assertAlmostEqual (for floats) check results and give a clear message when they fail.Lesson: Why we test, and a first test suite
  • Common mistake
    Tests must not depend on each other or on their order. test_add_more added a book, but test_total still saw only the pen, because setUp made a new cart for each test.Lesson: setUp, subTest and skip
  • Remember
    advice() receives the client as an argument (dependency injection), so a test can hand it a fake. Code that creates its own network client deep inside is much harder to test. Designing for testability means passing dependencies in.Lesson: Mocks: replacing what you cannot test
  • Common mistake
    100 % coverage means every line ran during the tests, NOT that every case was checked. The next lesson shows a bug that survives full coverage.Lesson: pytest: the most used test runner
  • In the exam
    All 8 example tests passed with 100 % coverage, yet price − price × 100 / 100 can come out a tiny bit below zero because of float rounding. The fix is price × (100 − percent) / 100, which gives exactly 0 at 100 %. The failing price changes from run to run, because Hypothesis tries random inputs.Lesson: Property based testing
  • Remember
    This shape, many fast unit tests at the bottom and few slow end to end tests at the top, is called the test pyramid. Run the fast tests on every save and all tests in CI (see the Git and CI/CD subject).Lesson: What to test and how much
3.3

Logging and debugging

Open chapter

log levels, loggers, handlers, formatters, habits, dictConfig, rotation, print, assert and pdb debugging.

Key ideas

  • Levels DEBUG 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30 (default), ERROR 40, CRITICAL 50. basicConfig(level=, format=, stream=, force=True).
  • Parts getLogger(__name__), logger and handler levels, Formatter fields (%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s), propagate to parents.
  • Habits logger.info("x %s", x) not f-strings, logger.exception in except, no secrets in logs, libraries never configure logging.
  • Configuration dictConfig once at start, RotatingFileHandler (maxBytes, backupCount), TimedRotatingFileHandler, QueueHandler.
  • Debugging f"{x=}", assert (removed by -O, not for input checks), breakpoint() and python -m pdb: b, c, n, s, p, l, w, q.

Formulas

Log volumeExam favourite
bytes = lines per second × bytes per line × seconds
50 lines a second of 200 bytes for a day (86,400 s) is 864,000,000 bytes, about 864 MB.
Lesson: The maths: log volume, rotation and bisecting
Disk used by a rotating logExam favourite
max size = (backupCount + 1) × maxBytes
maxBytes 1 MB with backupCount 4: at most 5 MB, for ever.
Lesson: The maths: log volume, rotation and bisecting
Levels shown for a given level L
shown = levels with number ≥ L
With WARNING (30): WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL, 3 of 5.
Lesson: The maths: log volume, rotation and bisecting
Sampling
lines kept = events / N when keeping 1 in N
1 in 100 of 2,000,000 requests: 20,000 lines.
Lesson: The maths: log volume, rotation and bisecting
Bisecting a bug (halving the suspect code)
checks = ⌈log2 n⌉
64 suspect lines: 6 checks with well placed prints or breakpoints.
Lesson: The maths: log volume, rotation and bisecting
Error budget
allowed failures = requests × (1 − target)
1,000,000 requests at 99.99 % success allow 100 failures. 120 ERROR lines use 120 % of the budget.
Lesson: The maths: log volume, rotation and bisecting

539Minimum Time DifferenceMediumTurn log times into minutes and sortChange each "HH:MM" into minutes, sort, and compare neighbours. Do not forget the gap that wraps around midnight: first + 1440 − last.
1418Display Table of Food Orders in a RestaurantMediumTurn order records into a report tableCount orders in a dict of table number to a dict of food to count. The header is "Table" plus the sorted food names. Rows go in number order of the tables.
165Compare Version NumbersMediumCompare number by numberSplit on dots, turn each part into an int (so 01 equals 1) and treat missing parts as 0.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    Without basicConfig the root logger shows only WARNING and above, on stderr. basicConfig sets the level, the format and the stream in one call, but only the first time, unless you pass force=True.Lesson: Logging: a diary for your program
  • Remember
    Loggers form a tree by name: shop.cart is a child of shop, which is a child of root. A record goes to the handlers of its logger and then, unless propagate is False, up to the parents. Add handlers in one place (often the root or the top package logger) and just call getLogger(__name__) in every module.Lesson: Loggers, handlers and formatters
  • In the exam
    Pass values as arguments: logger.debug("total %s", total). The text is only built if the record passes the level checks. An f-string is always built, even when the message is thrown away, as the first slow __str__ line shows.Lesson: Good logging habits
  • Common mistake
    Inside except, logger.exception("...") logs at ERROR level and adds the full traceback. Never log passwords, card numbers or personal data: logs are read by many people and kept for a long time.Lesson: Good logging habits
  • Remember
    Configure logging once, at program start, with dictConfig (or a file read into a dict, often YAML or TOML). Libraries must never call basicConfig: they only call getLogger(__name__), and the application decides what to show. dictConfig switches off loggers that already exist unless you set "disable_existing_loggers": False.Lesson: Configuring logging for a whole app
  • Remember
    On the second stop total is 70, not 70 + 0: the line replaces total instead of adding to it. The fix is total += s.Lesson: Debugging: print, assert and pdb
  • Common mistake
    assert checks a condition you believe is always true and raises AssertionError if not. Python started with -O skips every assert, so never use assert to check user input. Raise ValueError for that.Lesson: Debugging: print, assert and pdb

Step 4Advanced Python · Speed: complexity and smart data structures

4.1

Complexity, timing and profiling

Open chapter

Big O, operation costs, timeit, cProfile, memory, amortized cost and caching.

Key ideas

  • Big O Drop constants, keep the biggest term. Loops in a row add, nested loops multiply. O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2n).
  • Costs list: index O(1), append O(1) amortized, x in list O(n), insert(0)/pop(0) O(n). dict and set: O(1) average. sort O(n log n).
  • Measure timeit (python -m timeit -s setup stmt, best of several runs), time.perf_counter, realistic n.
  • Profile python -m cProfile -s cumulative file.py, tottime vs cumtime, fix only the hot spot. tracemalloc for memory, getsizeof is shallow.
  • Trade offs A better algorithm first. Sets for lookups, lru_cache for repeated work, generators to save memory.

Formulas

Definition of Big OExam favourite
f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are numbers c > 0 and n0 with f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for every n ≥ n0
3n + 5 = O(n): take c = 4 and n0 = 5, since 3n + 5 ≤ 4n when n ≥ 5.
Lesson: The maths behind Big O
Big Omega and Big Theta
Ω(g) is a lower bound, Θ(g) means both O(g) and Ω(g)
Comparison sorting is Ω(n log n): no comparison sort can do better.
Lesson: The maths behind Big O
Sum of a loop inside a loopExam favourite
1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / 2 = O(n²)
Comparing each item with the ones after it: 1000 items give 499,500 comparisons.
Lesson: The maths behind Big O
Geometric sum (doubling)Exam favourite
1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n = 2n − 1 < 2n
Copies for 1024 appends with doubling: 1 + 2 + ... + 512 = 1023, about 1 per append.
Lesson: The maths behind Big O
Halving
steps = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1
Binary search in 1,000,000 sorted items: at most 20 steps.
Lesson: The maths behind Big O
Master theoremExam favourite
T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(nd) gives O(nd) if d > logb a, O(nd log n) if d = logb a, O(nlogb a) if d < logb a
Merge sort: a = 2, b = 2, d = 1. log2 2 = 1 = d, so O(n log n).
Lesson: The maths behind Big O
Time estimate
seconds ≈ steps / (about 107 simple Python steps per second)
n = 105 with O(n²) is 1010 steps: about 1000 s. With O(n log n) it is 1.7 × 106: about 0.17 s.
Lesson: The maths behind Big O

219Contains Duplicate IIEasyRemember the last index of each valueA dict from value to its last index answers "where did I see this before" in O(1), so one pass is enough: O(n) instead of comparing all pairs.

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Look at the table: for 1000 items linear search needs 1000 steps, binary search only 10, and comparing every pair needs 1,000,000. The same computer, the same data size, and a 100,000 times difference.Lesson: Big O: how the work grows
  • Common mistake
    Hidden loops count too. x in my_list, my_list.index(x), my_list.remove(x), my_list.insert(0, x), "".join and slicing a[i:j] each walk through items. Putting one of them inside a loop is the most common way Python code becomes quadratic by accident.Lesson: Finding the Big O of code
  • In the exam
    Average case versus worst case: a dict lookup is O(1) on average, but if many keys had the same hash it could take O(n). Python adds random salt to str hashes so attackers cannot cause this on purpose. For interviews and exams, dict and set operations are O(1).Lesson: Finding the Big O of code
  • Remember
    60.9 microseconds against 19.4 nanoseconds: the set is about 3,000 times faster for 10,000 numbers. -s is the setup, which runs once and is not timed. timeit chooses how many loops to run and reports the best of 5 rounds.Lesson: Measuring with timeit
  • Remember
    slow_unique takes 0.136 of the 0.138 seconds, so that is the only function worth fixing. Speeding up anything else could save at most 0.002 seconds. Always profile before you optimise: the slow part is often not where you expect.Lesson: Finding the slow part with cProfile
  • In the exam
    sys.getsizeof is shallow. For a list it counts the list and its slots, not the objects inside, which is why a list holding a huge number has the same size as one holding a small number. tracemalloc counts every allocation made while it runs, so it shows the real memory a piece of code needed.Lesson: Memory: getsizeof, tracemalloc and generators
  • Remember
    Most appends cost one step. Now and then the array is full and must copy everything, which costs n steps. But because the space doubles each time, the copies add up to less than n in total, so the average (amortized) cost per append stays about 1. That is why list.append is called O(1) amortized.Lesson: Amortized cost and trading memory for time
  • Remember
    fib_slow(20) makes 21,891 calls because it works out the same values again and again. With lru_cache each value from 0 to 20 is computed once: 21 calls. We spend a little memory (21 stored answers) to save a huge amount of time, which is the idea behind dynamic programming.Lesson: Amortized cost and trading memory for time
4.2

collections, heapq and bisect

Open chapter

Counter, deque, namedtuple, OrderedDict, ChainMap, heapq priority queues and bisect.

Key ideas

  • Counter Counter(items), c[x] is 0 if missing, most_common(k), total(), elements(), + - & | on counts.
  • deque append, appendleft, pop, popleft all O(1), rotate(n), deque(maxlen=n). Queues and BFS use popleft.
  • Records namedtuple("P", ["x", "y"]) with _replace, _asdict, _fields. OrderedDict.move_to_end, popitem(last=False). ChainMap(first, fallback). defaultdict(list).
  • heapq heappush, heappop O(log n), heapify O(n), heap[0] smallest, nlargest and nsmallest O(n log k), merge, (priority, count, item), heappush_max in 3.14.
  • bisect bisect_left, bisect_right, insort, key= since 3.10. Range count = right(high) − left(low). Only on sorted lists.

Formulas

Heap indexesExam favourite
parent(i) = (i − 1) // 2, children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2
Index 4 has parent 1 and children 9 and 10.
Lesson: The maths: heap indexes, heights and costs
Height of a heapExam favourite
h = ⌊log2 n⌋
1,000,000 items: 19 levels below the top, so a push makes at most 19 swaps.
Lesson: The maths: heap indexes, heights and costs
heapify is O(n)
work ≤ ∑ (n / 2h+1) · h < n
Most items are near the bottom and move only a little, so the total is less than n swaps.
Lesson: The maths: heap indexes, heights and costs
Top k with a heapExam favourite
O(n log k) instead of O(n log n) for a full sort
k = 10 of n = 106: about 3.3 × 106 steps against 2 × 107.
Lesson: The maths: heap indexes, heights and costs
Binary search
comparisons ≤ ⌈log2(n + 1)⌉
1000 sorted items: at most 10 comparisons.
Lesson: The maths: heap indexes, heights and costs
Front removals from a list
shifts = (n − 1) + (n − 2) + ... + 1 = n(n − 1) / 2
Emptying 10,000 items with pop(0): about 5 × 107 shifts. With deque.popleft: 0.
Lesson: The maths: heap indexes, heights and costs

1046Last Stone WeightEasyA max-heap with negative numbersAlways smash the two heaviest stones. heapq is a min-heap, so store −weight. (Python 3.14 also has heappop_max, but LeetCode may run an older Python.)
1351Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted MatrixEasybisect on each rowEach row goes down from left to right. With key=lambda v: −v it goes up, so bisect finds where the negatives start in O(log n) per row.
215Kth Largest Element in an ArrayMediumA min-heap of size kKeep the k largest numbers seen so far in a min-heap. Its top is the kth largest. O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.

692Top K Frequent WordsMediumCounter, then sort by two keysCount with Counter. Sort by count going down, then by the word going up for ties: key=(-count, word).
2300Successful Pairs of Spells and PotionsMediumSort once, then bisect for each spellA spell s needs a potion of at least ⌈success / s⌉. Sort the potions and bisect_left gives how many are too weak. O((n + m) log m).
300Longest Increasing SubsequenceMediumPatience sorting with bisecttails[i] is the smallest last number of an increasing run of length i + 1. Each number replaces the first tail that is not smaller, found with bisect_left. O(n log n).
621Task SchedulerMediumCount the most common taskThe most common task (count m) needs m − 1 gaps of n slots after it. Tasks that share that top count fill the last row. The answer is never less than the number of tasks.
239Sliding Window MaximumHardA monotonic deque of indexesKeep indexes whose values go down from front to back. Drop smaller values from the back before adding, and the front once it leaves the window. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n).
295Find Median from Data StreamHardTwo heapsA max-heap (negative numbers) holds the smaller half, a min-heap the bigger half. Keep their sizes equal or the low half one bigger. The median is at the tops.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Counter is a dict subclass, so everything a dict can do works too. Unlike a dict, a missing key gives 0 instead of KeyError. most_common(k) returns the k most common items with their counts, and items with the same count keep the order in which they were first seen.Lesson: Counter: counting made easy
  • In the exam
    A deque (say "deck") is a double ended queue. Adding and removing at either end is O(1). A list does the same at the end, but list.insert(0, x) and list.pop(0) must shift every other item, which is O(n).Lesson: deque: a fast queue with two ends
  • Remember
    Breadth first search (BFS) always takes the oldest path from the front of the queue and adds new paths at the back. That is why it finds the path with the fewest steps first, and why it needs a deque, not a list.Lesson: deque: a fast queue with two ends
  • In the exam
    Since Python 3.7 every dict keeps insertion order. OrderedDict still has extras: move_to_end(key), popitem(last=False) for the oldest item, and == compares order too. That makes it the classic tool for an LRU cache.Lesson: namedtuple, OrderedDict, ChainMap and defaultdict
  • Remember
    ChainMap does not copy anything. It searches the dicts one after another, so a change to user is seen at once. Writes go to the first dict only. It is how Python looks up names: locals, then globals, then builtins.Lesson: namedtuple, OrderedDict, ChainMap and defaultdict
  • In the exam
    A heap is a list where every item is smaller than or equal to its two children: heap[i] ≤ heap[2i + 1] and heap[i] ≤ heap[2i + 2]. So heap[0] is always the smallest. The rest is NOT sorted. heappush and heappop are O(log n), heapify is O(n), and looking at heap[0] is O(1).Lesson: heapq: a priority queue in a list
  • Remember
    Put tuples like (priority, count, task) in a heap. Tuples compare item by item, so the priority decides first. The count (from itertools.count()) breaks ties, so two tasks with the same priority never have to be compared, which would fail for objects that cannot be compared.Lesson: heapq: a priority queue in a list
  • Remember
    bisect_right(a, x) − bisect_left(a, x) is how many times x appears. Counting values in a range or looking up which band a number falls into (grades, tax brackets, prices) are classic uses.Lesson: bisect: binary search in a sorted list

Step 5Advanced Python · Doing many things at once: threads, processes and asyncio

5.1

Threads and processes

Open chapter

threads, races and locks, worker queues, futures, the GIL, processes and free-threaded Python.

Key ideas

  • When to use what I/O bound: threads or asyncio. CPU bound: processes (or python3.14t). Measure first.
  • Threads Thread(target, args), start, join, daemon. Shared memory means races: protect with with lock:.
  • Sync tools Lock, RLock, Semaphore(n), Event, Condition, Barrier, queue.Queue. Same lock order everywhere to avoid deadlock.
  • Executors ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor: submit, map (keeps order), as_completed (finish order), result() raises errors.
  • Processes if __name__ == "__main__" guard, picklable functions and data, start methods fork, spawn, forkserver (Linux default in 3.14).

Formulas

Speedup and efficiencyExam favourite
S = T1 / Tn, E = S / n
1.30 s alone, 0.40 s with 4 processes: S = 3.25, E = 0.8125 (about 81 %).
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes
Amdahl's lawExam favourite
S(n) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n)
p = 0.9 of the work can run in parallel, n = 4: S = 1 / (0.1 + 0.225) ≈ 3.08.
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes
The limit of Amdahl's law
S(∞) = 1 / (1 − p)
With p = 0.9, even a million cores give at most 10 times.
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes
Gustafson's law
S(n) = n − (1 − p)(n − 1)
If the problem grows with the cores: n = 4, p = 0.9 gives 3.7.
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes
Threads for I/O workExam favourite
threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time)
4 cores, 90 ms waiting and 10 ms computing per job: 4 × 10 = 40 threads.
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes
Little's law
L = λ × W
200 requests per second that each take 0.25 s: 50 requests in progress, so about 50 workers.
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes
Lost updates
final = expected − lost
4 threads × 100 additions should give 400. Every overwrite loses one.
Lesson: The maths: speedup, Amdahl and pool sizes

Tips and traps

  • Remember
    Four downloads of 0.5 seconds take 2 seconds one by one but only 0.5 seconds with four threads, because the waiting happens at the same time. While a thread waits for I/O (sleep, network, files) it lets go of the GIL, so others can run.Lesson: Doing many things at once
  • Common mistake
    Every thread in a process shares the same global variables and objects. That makes it easy to pass data, and also easy to break data: two threads changing the same object at the same time is a race condition.Lesson: Threads: start, join and share
  • Common mistake
    counter = counter + 1 is really three steps: read, add, write. If another thread writes between your read and your write, your write wipes out its update. time.sleep(0) here forces a switch at the worst moment, but real programs hit the same bug by chance, often only under heavy load.Lesson: Race conditions and locks
  • In the exam
    A deadlock happens when thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B while thread 2 holds B and waits for A. Neither can go on. Prevent it by always taking locks in the same order, holding them briefly, or using a timeout.Lesson: Race conditions and locks
  • Remember
    queue.Queue does the locking for you. Producers put jobs in, worker threads get them out. get() waits when the queue is empty. Putting one None per worker is a common way to tell workers to stop.Lesson: Worker threads with queue and futures
  • In the exam
    With the GIL, 4 threads are no faster than one (1.37 s against 1.30 s). 4 processes are 3.3 times faster. The free-threaded build python3.14t (officially supported since 3.14) has no GIL, so there 4 threads are fast too.Lesson: The GIL and processes
5.2

asyncio: async and await

Open chapter

coroutines, the event loop, gather and TaskGroup, timeouts, limits, queues and httpx.

Key ideas

  • Basics async def, await (only inside async def), asyncio.run(main()) once. Calling a coroutine function does not run it.
  • Together gather (results in order), TaskGroup with except*, create_task (keep a reference), as_completed (finish order).
  • Control asyncio.timeout(s) and wait_for, task.cancel() and CancelledError (raise it again), Semaphore(k) to limit.
  • Pipelines asyncio.Queue(maxsize) with await put and get for back pressure. Async generators, async for, async with.
  • Never block No time.sleep or requests in coroutines. Use asyncio.sleep, httpx.AsyncClient, asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.

Formulas

Time one by oneExam favourite
T = n × t
20 requests of 0.2 s: 4 s.
Lesson: The maths: waits that overlap
Time with all at onceExam favourite
T ≈ max(ti) + overhead
20 requests of 0.2 s: about 0.2 s (measured 0.26 s).
Lesson: The maths: waits that overlap
With a limit of k at onceExam favourite
T ≈ ⌈n / k⌉ × t
20 requests, at most 5 at once, 0.2 s each: 4 rounds, 0.8 s.
Lesson: The maths: waits that overlap
Throughput
requests per second = k / t
5 at once, 0.2 s each: 25 requests per second.
Lesson: The maths: waits that overlap
Little's law for open connections
L = λ × W
1000 requests per second with 0.5 s waits: 500 tasks waiting at any moment.
Lesson: The maths: waits that overlap
Memory for many waiters
memory ≈ n × size of one waiter
10,000 tasks of about 2 KB is about 20 MB. 10,000 threads reserve about 80 GB of address space for stacks.
Lesson: The maths: waits that overlap

2621SleepEasyawait asyncio.sleepLeetCode asks this one in JavaScript. In Python asyncio the same idea is a coroutine that awaits asyncio.sleep(millis / 1000).
2723Add Two PromisesEasyAwait both at the same timeA JavaScript problem. In Python, gather awaits both coroutines at the same time and returns their values, so the total wait is the longer one, not the sum.
2648Generate Fibonacci SequenceEasyAn endless generatorA JavaScript generator problem. In Python, a while True loop with yield gives the numbers one at a time, and itertools.islice takes as many as you need.
2649Nested Array GeneratorMediumyield from for the nested listsA JavaScript generator problem. Walk the list, and for a nested list hand over to a recursive generator with yield from.

2721Execute Asynchronous Functions in ParallelMediumgather keeps the orderA JavaScript problem (write Promise.all without Promise.all). In Python, gather starts all of them, keeps the results in the order given and raises the first error.
2622Cache With Time LimitMediumStore the value with its end timeA JavaScript design problem. Keep key: (value, expires_at). A key counts only while the clock is before its end time. The clock is passed in so the tests do not have to wait.
2627DebounceMediumCancel the waiting call and schedule a new oneA JavaScript problem. With asyncio, loop.call_later schedules the call. A new call cancels the handle of the one still waiting.
2636Promise PoolMediumn workers share one iteratorA JavaScript problem. Start n worker coroutines that all take the next function from the same iterator. At most n functions run at any moment.
2650Design Cancellable FunctionHardDrive a generator by hand, race each wait against cancelA JavaScript problem, and exactly how await works inside: send each result into the generator, throw errors into it, and throw a Cancelled error if cancel() wins the race.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • Common mistake
    Calling make_tea(...) only creates a coroutine object, it runs nothing. The code runs when it is awaited, or when it is wrapped in a task (gather, create_task, TaskGroup). Forgetting await is the most common asyncio bug: Python warns "coroutine ... was never awaited".Lesson: asyncio: many waits in one thread
  • Common mistake
    Keep a reference to every task you create with create_task (in a list or a set), or use a TaskGroup. The loop holds tasks only weakly, so a task nobody refers to can disappear before it finishes.Lesson: Tasks, TaskGroup and as_completed
  • In the exam
    Cancelling a task raises CancelledError inside it at its current await. Clean up in finally blocks, and do not swallow CancelledError without raising it again, or the task cannot be stopped.Lesson: Timeouts, cancelling and limits
  • Remember
    A Semaphore limits how many tasks do something at once. Without it, gathering 10,000 downloads opens 10,000 connections at the same moment, which servers often punish by refusing or blocking you.Lesson: Timeouts, cancelling and limits
  • Remember
    asyncio.Queue is like queue.Queue, but put and get are awaited. With maxsize=2 the producer waits when two items are waiting. This back pressure stops a fast producer from filling memory while a slow consumer catches up.Lesson: Pipelines with asyncio.Queue
  • Remember
    20 × 0.2 s = 4 s one by one. With asyncio all 20 waits overlap, so it takes about one wait: 0.26 s, 16 times faster, in one thread.Lesson: Real network code, and blocking calls
  • Common mistake
    A normal blocking call (time.sleep, requests.get, a slow calculation) inside a coroutine freezes the whole loop. Use the async version (asyncio.sleep, httpx.AsyncClient, aiofiles), or push the blocking call to a thread with asyncio.to_thread, or to a process pool with loop.run_in_executor.Lesson: Real network code, and blocking calls

Step 6Advanced Python · The standard library toolbox: text, data, databases and GUIs

6.1

Regular expressions

Open chapter

regex syntax, the re functions, groups, sub and split, flags, greedy and lazy, lookarounds.

Key ideas

  • Syntax . \d \w \s [abc] [^abc] ^ $ \b, repeats * + ? {m,n}, lazy *? +?, | and ( ). Always raw strings.
  • Functions search (anywhere), match (start), fullmatch (whole), findall (strings), finditer (match objects), sub, subn, split.
  • Groups m.group(n), m.groups(), (?P<name>...), m.groupdict(), (?:...) non-capturing, \1 backreference, \g<name> in sub.
  • Flags IGNORECASE, MULTILINE, DOTALL, VERBOSE. re.compile for named patterns, re.escape for literal text.
  • Care Greedy versus lazy, lookarounds (?=) (?!) (?<=) (?

Formulas

Choices for a character classExam favourite
patterns of length n over a class of size k match kn strings
\d{4} matches 104 = 10,000 strings, 0000 to 9999.
Lesson: The maths: languages and automata
A range of repeats
[ab]{1,3} matches 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 strings
∑ ki for i from min to max.
Lesson: The maths: languages and automata
Positions tried by search
up to n + 1 starting places
Text of length 17: starts 0 to 17.
Lesson: The maths: languages and automata
A regular languageExam favourite
built from single characters with union (|), concatenation and star (*)
Every such pattern can be matched by a finite automaton with no memory.
Lesson: The maths: languages and automata
Catastrophic backtrackingExam favourite
ways to split n letters among nested repeats grows like 2n
(a+)+$ on 30 a's followed by "!": about 230 ≈ 109 tries.
Lesson: The maths: languages and automata
Linear time engines
time = O(m × n) for pattern size m and text size n
RE2 and Rust's regex guarantee this, Python's re does not.
Lesson: The maths: languages and automata

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    Use fullmatch to check input such as a postcode or a username. search would also accept "xx12345yy" because it finds 12345 inside it.Lesson: search, match, fullmatch, findall, finditer
  • Common mistake
    findall changes what it returns when the pattern has groups: with one group it returns that group's text, with several it returns tuples. Use (?:...) for groups you only need for | or repeats.Lesson: Groups: pulling parts out
  • Remember
    re.compile(pattern) gives a pattern object with the same methods. re caches recent patterns, so compiling is mostly about clarity: give a long pattern a name and write it once.Lesson: sub, split, flags and compile
  • Common mistake
    Some patterns make the engine try a huge number of ways before failing, for example (a+)+$ on "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!". This is catastrophic backtracking, and attackers use it to freeze servers (ReDoS). Avoid nested repeats of the same thing, or use possessive quantifiers.Lesson: Greedy, lazy, anchors and lookarounds
  • Remember
    A named, verbose pattern reads like documentation. fullmatch makes sure the line has exactly the expected shape, and broken lines are skipped instead of giving wrong data.Lesson: Parsing real text

CSV, JSON, XML and settings files

Open chapter

Tips and traps

  • In the exam

6.3

Databases with sqlite3 and SQL

Open chapter

sqlite3, SQL queries and joins, placeholders against injection, transactions, constraints and indexes.

Key ideas

  • Basics sqlite3.connect(path or ":memory:"), execute, executemany, executescript, commit, close, fetchone, fetchall, lastrowid, rowcount.
  • SQL CREATE TABLE, INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE with WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, JOIN, LEFT JOIN, COUNT, SUM, COALESCE, LIMIT.
  • Safety Values only through ? or :name. Never f-strings in SQL. Check table and column names against a fixed list.
  • Transactions "with conn:" commits or rolls back (does not close). IntegrityError from PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, foreign keys (PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON).
  • Speed sqlite3.Row, CREATE INDEX, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SCAN vs SEARCH), one commit for many inserts, B-tree height log base f of N.

Formulas

Full scan
cost ≈ N rows read
Finding one user among 1,000,000 without an index reads 1,000,000 rows.
Lesson: The maths: indexes, joins and estimates
B-tree heightExam favourite
h = ⌈logf N⌉, f = keys per page (fan out)
N = 1,000,000 and f = 100: h = 3 page reads instead of a million rows.
Lesson: The maths: indexes, joins and estimates
Binary search in a sorted index
comparisons ≈ ⌈log2 N⌉
log2 1,000,000 ≈ 20.
Lesson: The maths: indexes, joins and estimates
Selectivity of WHERE a = vExam favourite
rows ≈ N / V(a), V(a) = number of different values
1,000,000 rows and 100 cities: about 10,000 rows per city.
Lesson: The maths: indexes, joins and estimates
Equi join size estimate
|R ⋈ S| ≈ |R| × |S| / max(V(R, a), V(S, a))
1000 customers, 5000 orders, joined on 1000 customer ids: 1000 × 5000 / 1000 = 5000 rows.
Lesson: The maths: indexes, joins and estimates
Cost of commits
time ≈ commits × time per disk sync
1000 inserts with 1000 commits at 5 ms each: 5 s. One commit: about 5 ms.

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    The most common beginner bug: INSERT works, the program ends, and the data is gone. You forgot conn.commit(). Using "with conn:" commits for you.Lesson: Connect, execute, commit, fetch
  • Remember
    SQL types in SQLite are flexible: INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and NULL. Python int, float, str, bytes and None map to them. Store dates as ISO text such as "2026-11-07", because the automatic date converters are deprecated since Python 3.12.Lesson: Connect, execute, commit, fetch
  • Common mistake
    An UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes EVERY row. Write the WHERE first, and try it as a SELECT before you run it.Lesson: SQL in one lesson: SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY
  • Common mistake
    Never put values into SQL with f-strings, +, % or .format(). Use ? or :name every time. Placeholders stop SQL injection, handle quotes in names like O'Neil, and let the database reuse the prepared statement.Lesson: Placeholders and SQL injection
  • In the exam
    Placeholders are for VALUES only. A table or column name cannot be a ?. If a user picks the column to sort by, check it against a fixed list such as {"name", "price"} before you put it into the SQL.Lesson: Placeholders and SQL injection
  • Remember
    "with conn:" commits or rolls back, but it does NOT close the connection. Since Python 3.12 you can also pass autocommit=False to sqlite3.connect for the transaction rules of the database standard (PEP 249).Lesson: Transactions and rules on the data
  • Remember
    An index is a sorted copy of one column with a pointer to each row, kept in a B-tree. It turns a scan of every row into a few page reads. It costs disk space and makes INSERT and UPDATE a little slower, so index the columns you search, join or sort by often.Lesson: Friendlier rows and fast lookups with indexes
6.4

Desktop windows with tkinter

Open chapter

tkinter widgets, layouts, variables, events, Canvas animation with after() and responsive apps.

Key ideas

  • First window root = tk.Tk(), title, geometry("WxH"), Label, Button(command=f), pack, root.mainloop(). command=f without brackets.
  • Layout grid(row, column, sticky="nsew", columnspan, padx, pady), columnconfigure(i, weight=1), pack(side, fill, expand), place(x, y). One manager per parent.
  • Input and variables Entry.get, insert, delete. StringVar, IntVar, BooleanVar, textvariable, variable, trace_add("write", f). messagebox, filedialog.
  • Events and Canvas bind("", f) with event.x, event.y, event.keysym. create_line, create_oval, move, coords. after(ms, f) for animation.
  • Responsive apps Callbacks return fast. after() for timers, threads plus queue.Queue for slow work, widgets only from the main thread. Model apart from the view.

Formulas

Screen coordinates
x grows to the right, y grows DOWN, (0, 0) is the top left corner
A point 50 pixels from the top has y = 50, not y = height − 50.
Lesson: The maths: pixels, frames and how fast people click
Centre a windowExam favourite
x = (screen width − window width) // 2, y = (screen height − window height) // 2
A 300 × 200 window on 1920 × 1080: x = 810, y = 440, geometry "300x200+810+440".
Lesson: The maths: pixels, frames and how fast people click
Frames and speed
delay = 1000 / fps ms, speed = pixels per step × 1000 / delay
after(20, ...) gives 50 frames a second. 4 pixels a step is 200 pixels a second.
Lesson: The maths: pixels, frames and how fast people click
Sharing extra space
extra for column i = extra × weighti / sum of weights
300 extra pixels, weights 1 and 2: 100 and 200 pixels.
Lesson: The maths: pixels, frames and how fast people click
Fitts's lawExam favourite
time = a + b × log2(D / W + 1)
D = distance to the target, W = its width. Big, close buttons are faster to hit.
Lesson: The maths: pixels, frames and how fast people click
Hick's law
time = b × log2(n + 1)
n equal choices. 7 menu items: log2 8 = 3 times b.
Lesson: The maths: pixels, frames and how fast people click

657Robot Return to OriginEasyCount the moves in each directionLike moving an item on a canvas: R adds to x, L takes away. Back at the start means x and y are both 0.
733Flood FillEasyThe paint bucket tool: breadth first searchStart at the clicked pixel and paint every neighbour (up, down, left, right) that has the old colour. Stop at once if the new colour equals the old one.
836Rectangle OverlapEasyOverlap on both axesTwo boxes overlap when the left edge of each is before the right edge of the other, on x AND on y. Touching edges do not count. Games use this for collisions.
1232Check If It Is a Straight LineEasyCompare slopes with a cross productPoints are on one line when (y - y0) × (x1 - x0) equals (y1 - y0) × (x - x0) for every point. Multiplying avoids dividing by zero for vertical lines.
223Rectangle AreaMediumBoth areas minus the overlapAdd the two areas and take away the overlap. The overlap width is max(0, min of right edges minus max of left edges), the same for the height.
593Valid SquareMediumSix distances between four pointsA square has 4 equal sides and 2 equal, longer diagonals. Use squared distances to stay with whole numbers, and reject a length of 0.
874Walking Robot SimulationMediumDirections as a list, obstacles as a setKeep the four directions in a list and turn by moving the index. Store obstacles as a set of tuples so each step is checked in O(1).
1041Robot Bounded In CircleMediumRun the instructions once and look at the resultAfter one run the robot is either back at the start or facing a new direction. In both cases it stays in a circle. Only "away and still facing north" escapes.
391Perfect RectangleHardAreas add up and only four corners stayThe small areas must add up to the big box. Toggle every corner in a set: inner corners appear an even number of times and cancel out, so exactly the four outer corners must be left.
850Rectangle Area IIHardCoordinate compression on a gridCollect every x and y edge, sort them and mark which small cells between them are covered. Add up the covered cells and take the result modulo 109 + 7.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    command=say_hello() (with brackets) is the classic beginner bug: it calls the function ONCE while the button is made and stores its result, None, as the command. Then clicks do nothing. To pass arguments, use command=lambda: say(name).Lesson: Your first window
  • Common mistake
    Never mix pack and grid for widgets with the same parent: Tk raises TclError ("cannot use geometry manager grid inside . which already has slaves managed by pack"). Put each group in its own Frame instead, and each Frame can use its own manager.Lesson: Placing widgets: pack, grid and place
  • Remember
    ttk widgets (from tkinter import ttk) use the look of the operating system and are styled with themes. The older tk widgets use options such as bg and fg. Prefer ttk where it has the widget. Listbox, Text, Canvas and Menu exist only in tk.Lesson: Widgets and control variables
  • Remember
    bind on a widget catches events in that widget. root.bind catches them anywhere in the window, and bind_all in every window of the program. For the close button use root.protocol("WM_DELETE_WINDOW", function).Lesson: Events, the Canvas and animation with after()
  • Common mistake
    Tk is not thread safe. Create and change widgets only in the thread that runs mainloop. Other threads hand their results over through a queue, and the main thread picks them up with after().Lesson: Long tasks without freezing the window

Step 8Advanced Python · Exam practice

8.1

Exam practice: PCPP1 style papers

Open chapter

Four PCPP1 style papers, a bug hunt, the traps table, exam technique and a mock quiz.

Key ideas

  • Exam facts PCPP1 (PCPP-32-101) as listed by training providers: 45 questions, 65 minutes, 70 %. Confirm on pythoninstitute.org/pcpp1.
  • Object traps __eq__ needs __hash__, NotImplemented for unknown types, super() follows the MRO, wraps keeps the name, slots remove __dict__.
  • Iteration traps Generators run lazily and once, send resumes a yield, yield from returns the inner value, groupby needs sorted input.
  • Error traps __exit__ True swallows, raise from sets __cause__, except* splits groups, never except Exception: pass.
  • Library traps Raw strings for regex, json makes lists and str keys, csv gives str, commit() in sqlite3, command=f in tkinter.

Formulas

Safety margin
aim = pass mark + 15 points in practice
Practise until you score about 85 %, because exam nerves cost a few points.

Table: no. · problem · level · pattern
No.ProblemLevelPatternHint
304Range Sum Query 2D - ImmutableMediumA class with a table of prefix sumsBuild sums[r + 1][c + 1] = the total of the rectangle from (0, 0) to (r, c) once in __init__. Any rectangle is then four lookups.
438Find All Anagrams in a StringMediumA sliding window of CountersKeep a Counter of the last len(p) letters. Add the new letter, remove the oldest, and compare with the Counter of p.
39Combination SumMediumA recursive generatorA generator yields each combination as soon as it is found. Pass the start index so a number is never used before a smaller one, which avoids repeats.
131Palindrome PartitioningMediumyield from for every first pieceTry every palindrome as the first piece, then partition the rest the same way. A generator with yield from keeps the code short.
1143Longest Common SubsequenceMediumRecursion with lru_cachebest(i, j) compares text1[i:] and text2[j:]. Equal letters add 1, otherwise skip one letter on either side. functools.cache stores every answer.
221Maximal SquareMediumGrow squares from three neighbourssize[r][c] is the side of the biggest all "1" square ending at (r, c): 1 + the smallest of the sizes above, to the left and diagonal.
72Edit DistanceMediumA table of smaller answersdist[i][j] is the cost to turn the first i letters of word1 into the first j letters of word2. Equal letters cost nothing, otherwise 1 + the best of insert, delete or replace.
42Trapping Rain WaterHardTwo pointers with the highest wall on each sideWater above a bar is the lower of the highest walls on its left and right, minus the bar. Move the pointer on the lower side, because that side decides the water level.
76Minimum Window SubstringHardGrow the window, then shrink itMove the right end until the window holds every letter of t (count with a Counter). Then move the left end while it still does, and remember the shortest window.
460LFU CacheHardA dict of OrderedDicts, one per use countKeep the value and the use count of each key, and an OrderedDict of keys for every count. Evict the oldest key in the group with the smallest count.

    Cover the answers, write down what you think each line prints, then open the answers. A wrong guess tells you exactly which chapter to reread.Lesson: The PCPP1 exam and how to use this chapter

    In the exam: read the whole snippet first, then the options. Trace it on paper and watch for the answer "the code raises an exception". Mark hard questions and come back, because every question is worth the same.Lesson: Exam technique and a study plan

Step 1Web and APIs · How the web works: HTTP, REST and sockets

1.1

HTTP and REST: how the web talks

Open chapter

HTTP messages, URLs, methods, status codes, headers, cookies, caching and REST design.

Key ideas

  • Messages Request line (method, path, version), headers, blank line, body. Status line, headers, blank line, body. \r\n line ends.
  • Methods and codes GET read, POST create (201 + Location), PUT replace, PATCH change, DELETE (204). 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client, 5xx server.
  • URLs urlsplit, parse_qs, parse_qsl, urlencode, quote, urljoin. Percent encoding: one byte becomes %XX.
  • Headers Content-Type, Accept, Authorization, Set-Cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match for 304.
  • Python http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler (do_GET, send_response, send_header, end_headers, wfile), urllib.request, HTTPError for 4xx and 5xx.

Formulas

Time to first byteExam favourite
about (TCP 1 + TLS 1 + request 1) round trips × RTT
RTT 50 ms: 3 × 50 = 150 ms before the first byte of the answer, however small it is.
Lesson: The maths: latency, bandwidth and caching
Transfer time
time = size × 8 / bandwidth
2 MB at 40 Mbit/s: 16 Mbit / 40 = 0.4 s.
Lesson: The maths: latency, bandwidth and caching
Average time with a cacheExam favourite
average = hit rate × hit time + (1 − hit rate) × miss time
80 % hits at 5 ms, misses at 200 ms: 0.8 × 5 + 0.2 × 200 = 44 ms.
Lesson: The maths: latency, bandwidth and caching
Little's law
requests in progress = arrival rate × time per request
200 requests a second, 50 ms each: 10 requests at the same moment.
Lesson: The maths: latency, bandwidth and caching
Bandwidth delay product
bits in flight = bandwidth × RTT
100 Mbit/s and 80 ms: 8 Mbit (1 MB) on the wire at once.
Lesson: The maths: latency, bandwidth and caching
Percent encoding size
a byte outside the allowed set becomes 3 characters
"é" is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so it becomes 6 characters: %C3%A9.
Lesson: The maths: latency, bandwidth and caching

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    URLs may only contain a small set of characters. Others, like spaces, é or & inside a value, must be percent encoded: each byte becomes % and two hex digits, so a space is %20 and é (2 bytes in UTF-8) is %C3%A9. Use urlencode or let requests do it with params=, never glue query text together by hand.Lesson: URLs: the address of a resource
  • Remember
    BaseHTTPRequestHandler answers with HTTP/1.0 unless you set protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1" in the class. Every line ends with \r\n (carriage return and new line), and an empty line separates the headers from the body.Lesson: Inside an HTTP message
  • In the exam
    urllib.request.urlopen raises HTTPError for 4xx and 5xx answers. The requests library in the next chapters does not: it returns the response, and you call raise_for_status() when you want an exception.Lesson: REST: designing an API with resources
  • Common mistake
    HTTP itself has no memory between requests. Logins work because the server gives the browser a session cookie or a token, and the client sends it back every time. Mark session cookies HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, as in the example.Lesson: Headers, cookies and caching
1.2

Sockets, TCP and UDP: under HTTP

Open chapter

TCP and UDP sockets, bytes and struct, message framing, many clients with asyncio, IP addresses and subnets.

Key ideas

  • Sockets socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM) for TCP, SOCK_DGRAM for UDP. An address is (host, port). Ports 0 to 65,535. 127.0.0.1 local only, 0.0.0.0 every network card.
  • TCP calls Server: bind, listen, accept (new socket per client). Client: create_connection(addr, timeout). sendall, recv(n) gives 1 to n bytes, b"" means closed.
  • Framing TCP keeps no message borders. Length prefix with struct.pack("!I", n), or an end marker such as a new line. Loop until a message is complete.
  • UDP sendto and recvfrom, no handshake, borders kept, may lose or reorder. Used for DNS, games, video. 8 byte header.
  • Numbers MSS = MTU − 40. throughput ≤ window / RTT. window = bandwidth × RTT. /n network has 232 − n addresses.

Formulas

Addresses in a networkExam favourite
addresses = 232 − prefix, usable = addresses − 2
/24: 256 addresses, 254 usable. /20: 4,096 addresses.
Lesson: The maths: windows, round trips and loss
Data in one packet
MSS = MTU − IP header − TCP header
1,500 − 20 − 20 = 1,460 bytes of your data.
Lesson: The maths: windows, round trips and loss
Window limit on speedExam favourite
throughput ≤ window / RTT
A 64 KB window with RTT 100 ms: 65,535 × 8 / 0.1 ≈ 5.2 Mbit/s, however fast the line is.
Lesson: The maths: windows, round trips and loss
Window needed
window = bandwidth × RTT (the bandwidth delay product)
100 Mbit/s and 50 ms: 100,000,000 × 0.05 / 8 = 625,000 bytes.
Lesson: The maths: windows, round trips and loss
TCP with loss (Mathis formula)Exam favourite
throughput ≈ (MSS / RTT) × 1.22 / √p
MSS 1,460 B, RTT 100 ms, loss p = 0.0001: about 14.2 Mbit/s.
Lesson: The maths: windows, round trips and loss
Chance of at least one loss
P = 1 − (1 − p)n
100 packets with p = 0.01: 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 0.634.
Lesson: The maths: windows, round trips and loss

No.ProblemLevelPatternHint
190Reverse BitsEasyTake the last bit, push it in from the rightByte order and bit order matter on the wire. Take the lowest bit of n 32 times and add it to the result from the other end.
1971Find if Path Exists in GraphEasyBreadth first search from the sourceCan a packet get from one computer to another? Keep a set of visited computers and a queue of computers to visit.
2073Time Needed to Buy TicketsEasyCount what each person buys before k is doneA queue served in turns, like a server that sends one piece to each client in turn. People before k buy at most tickets[k], people after k at most tickets[k] minus 1.
743Network Delay TimeMediumDijkstra with a heapA signal spreads from computer k over links with delays. Dijkstra finds the fastest time to each computer, and the answer is the slowest of those.
1319Number of Operations to Make Network ConnectedMediumUnion find counts the groupsYou need at least n minus 1 cables. If there are enough, the answer is the number of separate groups minus 1.
1514Path with Maximum ProbabilityMediumDijkstra on the largest productEach link delivers a packet with some probability. Use a heap of negative probabilities so the most likely path comes out first.
787Cheapest Flights Within K StopsMediumBellman Ford for k + 1 roundsLike a packet with a hop limit (TTL). Each round allows one more flight. Copy the prices first so one round uses only one more flight.
1615Maximal Network RankMediumDegrees of both cities, minus 1 if they are linkedThe rank of two cities is the number of roads touching either one. Try every pair and do not count a shared road twice.
1192Critical Connections in a NetworkHardTarjan: discovery time and lowest reachable timeA cable is critical if cutting it splits the network. In a depth first search, the link to a child is critical when the child cannot reach back above itself.
1579Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully TraversableHardTwo union finds, shared edges firstUse the edges both Alice and Bob can use first, then each person's own edges. Every edge that joins nothing new can be removed.
Lesson: LeetCode practice

Tips and traps

  • In the exam
    A socket only knows bytes. Turn text into bytes with .encode("utf-8") before sending and back with .decode("utf-8") after receiving. "é" is one letter but 2 bytes, so always measure the length of the bytes, never of the text.Lesson: Bytes: what really travels
  • Common mistake
    Host "127.0.0.1" (localhost) only accepts connections from the same computer. "0.0.0.0" accepts them from every network card, so other computers can connect. Use 127.0.0.1 while you learn.Lesson: A TCP client and server
  • Common mistake
    A very common bug: the sender calls sendall twice and the receiver expects two recv calls to return the two messages. On a fast local test it often works, and then it fails on a real network. recv only promises "some bytes", so always loop until you have a whole message.Lesson: TCP is a stream: framing messages
  • Remember
    A UDP datagram larger than the path allows (about 1,472 bytes of data on normal Ethernet) gets split by IP, and if one piece is lost the whole datagram is lost. Keep UDP messages small.Lesson: UDP: single packets, no promises
  • In the exam
    A /24 network has 232 − 24 = 256 addresses. The first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, so 254 are left for computers. Ports go from 0 to 65,535, and ports below 1024 usually need admin rights.Lesson: IP addresses, ports and layers

Step 2Web and APIs · Calling web APIs

2.1

Calling web APIs with requests

Open chapter

requests: GET and POST, params and json, timeouts, errors, sessions, auth and JSON answers.

Key ideas

  • Calls requests.get, post, put, patch, delete(url, params=, json=, data=, headers=, timeout=). Response: status_code, ok, headers, text, content, json().
  • Errors raise_for_status() for 4xx and 5xx. HTTPError, ConnectionError, Timeout, JSONDecodeError, all under RequestException (catch it last).
  • Timeouts No default timeout. timeout=5 or timeout=(connect, read). Always pass one.
  • Session Reuses connections, keeps cookies and headers. Auth: Authorization: Bearer token, auth=(user, pw), API key header. Secrets come from environment variables.
  • JSON object to dict, array to list, null to None. [] for required keys, .get() for optional. datetime.fromisoformat for dates.

Formulas

Pages to fetchExam favourite
pages = ⌈items / page size⌉
95 items, 20 per page: ⌈4.75⌉ = 5 requests.
Lesson: The maths: round trips, timeouts and limits
Time without a Session
n × (handshake RTTs + 1) × RTT
10 calls, 2 handshake RTTs, RTT 50 ms: 10 × 3 × 50 = 1,500 ms.
Lesson: The maths: round trips, timeouts and limits
Time with a SessionExam favourite
(handshake RTTs + n) × RTT
(2 + 10) × 50 = 600 ms, so 900 ms saved.
Lesson: The maths: round trips, timeouts and limits
Longest wait with timeout=(c, r)
up to c + r for each silent stretch
timeout=(3, 2): up to 3 s to connect, then 2 s with no data before ReadTimeout.
Lesson: The maths: round trips, timeouts and limits
Rate limit
minimum time = requests / allowed rate
300 calls at 60 per minute: 5 minutes.
Lesson: The maths: round trips, timeouts and limits
Chance one of k tries worksExam favourite
P = 1 − (1 − p)k
p = 0.9, k = 3: 1 − 0.001 = 0.999.
Lesson: The maths: round trips, timeouts and limits

Tips and traps

  • Common mistake
    Always pass timeout=. requests has no timeout by default, so a server that never answers keeps your program waiting for ever. A number such as timeout=5 is used for connecting and again for each wait while reading.Lesson: Your first GET request
  • Remember
    For a big download use requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=10) and write for chunk in r.iter_content(64_000) into a file opened with "wb". Then the whole file never has to fit in memory.Lesson: Sending data: POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE
  • In the exam
    A Session keeps cookies and default headers, and it reuses the TCP (and TLS) connection for every request to the same host. The example shows 3 requests over 1 connection. That saves one or two round trips each time, so use a Session whenever you make more than a couple of calls.Lesson: Sessions, cookies and authentication
  • Common mistake
    Never put a real token or password in code that you share or commit to git. Read it with os.environ["API_TOKEN"] and keep it in a .env file that git ignores.Lesson: Sessions, cookies and authentication
  • Remember
    Use data["key"] when the key must be there (a missing key is a bug you want to see), and data.get("key", default) when it is optional. The next chapter shows pydantic, which checks the whole shape of an answer at once.Lesson: Working with JSON answers
2.2

Real API work: pages, retries, limits and validation

Open chapter

Pagination, retries with backoff and jitter, rate limits, pydantic validation and async calls with httpx.

Key ideas

  • Pages Loop with a generator until no next page or cursor. Cursors stay correct when data changes. pages = ⌈items / size⌉.
  • Retries Only timeouts, connection errors, 429, 502, 503, 504, and only idempotent requests. wait = random(0, min(cap, base × 2n)). Stop after k tries.
  • Limits 429 plus Retry-After (seconds or a date). Token bucket: capacity for bursts, rate for the average. X-RateLimit-Remaining.
  • pydantic class M(BaseModel), Field(min_length=, ge=, le=), M.model_validate(dict), model_dump(), TypeAdapter(list[M]).validate_json(text), ValidationError.errors().
  • httpx httpx.Client like a Session, httpx.AsyncClient with await, asyncio.gather for many, asyncio.Semaphore(n) to limit them.

Formulas

Backoff waitExam favourite
waitn = min(cap, base × 2n)
base 0.5 s: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 s for n = 0 to 4.
Lesson: The maths: backoff, limits and pages
Total backoff time
base × (2k − 1) for k waits
base 1 s, 4 waits: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 s.
Lesson: The maths: backoff, limits and pages
Full jitter
wait = random(0, base × 2n), mean = base × 2n / 2
n = 3, base 1 s: random between 0 and 8 s, 4 s on average.
Lesson: The maths: backoff, limits and pages
Token bucket in time TExam favourite
at most capacity + rate × T calls
rate 5/s, capacity 20, 10 s: 20 + 50 = 70 calls.
Lesson: The maths: backoff, limits and pages
Rows skipped by an offset
skipped = (page − 1) × size
page 50, size 20: 980 rows read and thrown away.
Lesson: The maths: backoff, limits and pages
Calls in flight (Little's law)Exam favourite
L = rate × time per call
100 calls/s at 0.25 s each: 25 at the same moment.
Lesson: The maths: backoff, limits and pages

Tables

Table: · no retry · fixed wait · exponential backoff
No retryFixed waitExponential backoffBackoff with jitter
